records.content: Data assimilation is the problem of estimating the state of a dynamical system given partial, noisy observations and prior knowledge. It sits at the intersection of Bayesian inference, optimisation and numerical analysis; the prior comes from a physical model (or a learned one), the likelihood comes from instruments, and the posterior is what we want.

Let x \in \mathbb{R}^n denote the state and y \in \mathbb{R}^m the observations. Bayes’ theorem gives the posteriorp(x \mid y) \propto p(y \mid x) p(x)

which has three ingredients:

Prior p(x). What we know about the state before seeing the data. Most commonly it is Gaussian, x \sim \mathcal{N}(x_b, B) (

(4.1)), with background mean x_b and background-error covariance B. In FourDVarNet the prior is replaced by a learned autoencoder; in AmortizedPosterior it is absorbed into the trained head.

Likelihood p(y \mid x). How observations relate to the state. Chapter 2 models them as H(x) plus Gaussian noise with covariance R (

(2.1)), so p(y \mid x) = \mathcal{N}(y; H(x), R), where the observation operator H maps state space to observation space.

Posterior p(x \mid y). What we infer about the state given the data. For a Gaussian prior and a Gaussian likelihood with linear H it is Gaussian in closed form (

(4.3), chapter 4); otherwise we approximate it.

The maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimator minimises the negative log-posterior,x^* = \underset{x}{\arg\min} \left\{-\log p(y \mid x) - \log p(x)\right\}

and with the Gaussian prior and likelihood above the bracket is, up to a constant, the 3DVar cost 

(5.1) of chapter 5. When the state evolves through dynamics M_t, we add a time index and a forward rollout, which gives 4DVar (chapters 6 to 8).

Consider a state x_0 at the start of an assimilation window and observations y_t at times t = 0, 1, \ldots, T. A dynamical model M_t propagates x_0 forward,x_t = M_t(x_0)

where x_t is the state at time t.

The 4D variational cost adds an observation term for every time to the background term. In strong-constraint 4DVar (chapter 6) the dynamics are exact, the control variable is x_0 alone and the cost is 

(6.1). In weak-constraint 4DVar (chapter 7) each step carries a model error \eta_t with covariance Q_t, the cost 

(7.2) gains a model-error term, and the control becomes the augmented vector (x_0, \eta_1, \ldots, \eta_T).

In the linear-Gaussian limit (linear H_t, linear M_t, Gaussian B,
R_t, Q_t) the posterior is Gaussian in closed form. In all other
cases we minimise J iteratively. The cost itself is the same; the
solver is where the methods diverge.

vardax implements seven peer methods, each specialising the general
problem above:

Method

Setting

Solver

OptimalInterpolation

Linear H, Gaussian B, R; T = 0

Closed-form

ThreeDVar

Nonlinear H; T = 0

optimistix minimiser

StrongFourDVar

Multi-time; dynamics treated as exact

optimistix minimiser + diffrax adjoint

WeakFourDVar

Multi-time; model error active

Same, augmented control

IncrementalFourDVar

Operational fast path of StrongFourDVar

GN outer + CG inner

FourDVarNet

Learned prior + learned grad modulator

Learned inner iteration

AmortizedPosterior

Direct q_\phi(x \mid y) head

Single forward pass

ReducedBasisFourDVar is StrongFourDVar with the control moved into a reduced basis, x_0 = x_b + \Phi X (see 

chapter 23). It was called Incremental4DVar before 0.1.11; that name is deprecated.

They are siblings, not subclasses, and each one is appropriate to a different regime.

records.content:
The dynamics M_t and the observation operator H_t are the physics. vardax does not own them; somax (geophysics), plumax (atmospheric transport and methane) or any user code can supply them, as long as they satisfy pipekit_cycle.ForwardModel and pipekit_cycle.ObservationOperator respectively.

This means the same analysis class accepts any forward. A
StrongFourDVar doesn’t know whether M_t is a shallow-water solver
from somax, a Lagrangian particle simulator from plumax, or a
neural emulator trained from physics outputs. The interface is fixed;
the implementation is a slot.

This separation is what makes vardax composable with the broader
JAX ecosystem (diffrax, optimistix, lineax, gaussx,
pipekit-cycle) without bespoke per-method wiring.

The four computations that recur in every DA method:

Forward model rollout 

(1.3). ODE integration via diffrax; vardax composes it but does not implement it.

Tangent-linear and adjoint M'_t, M'^\top_t. Computed via diffrax.AbstractAdjoint (recursive checkpointing, continuous backsolve or forward sensitivity; see chapter 12).

Observation operator H_t(x_t) and its tangent linear H'_t.
See chapter 2 (linearize() contract via lineax).

Inner minimisation \arg\min_x J(x). Via
optimistix.AbstractMinimiser (Gauss-Newton, BFGS, NonlinearCG,
fixed-point iteration). For incremental 4DVar, \arg\min is done by
CG on the linearised quadratic subproblem.

Each computation is owned by an upstream library. vardax composes them
into DA algorithms; it does not reimplement them.

A MAP x^* is the start of the answer, not the end. Real DA produces a posterior (mean, covariance and provenance) that downstream consumers (population models, alert systems, decision pipelines) need.

vardax exposes a Posterior(mean, cov, samples, provenance) container
returned by every analysis. Approximations include the Laplace
(LaplaceCovariance) at MAP, the Gauss-Newton Hessian inversion
(GaussNewtonHessian, free for IncrementalFourDVar), the ensemble
covariance (EnsembleCovariance via filterax), or direct sampling
from amortized heads. See chapter 13.

For the closed-form case (OptimalInterpolation) the posterior is exact, with the covariance 

(4.5) derived in chapter 4.

Chapters 1 to 3 establish the shared foundation: this chapter (the problem), chapter 2 (the observation model) and chapter 3 (the dynamical model and its adjoint).

Chapters 4 to 10 cover one analysis method each, in the order of the table above, from OptimalInterpolation in chapter 4 to AmortizedPosterior in chapter 10, so in increasing order of sophistication.

Chapters 11 to 14 cover cross-cutting concerns: observation operators (the averaging-kernel and multi-instrument family), adjoint composition via optimistix and diffrax, posterior covariance, and the six-step research-to-operations methodology.

Chapters 15 to 17 are end-to-end examples on Lorenz, SSH and methane.

The companion design docs in 

design/ document the API
contracts and architectural decisions behind these methods.

The observation operator H : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m maps the state x to predicted observations \hat{y} = H(x). Real instruments rarely measure the state directly; they smooth, average, mask or project it. Getting H right is what separates an inversion that recovers the truth from one that returns a biased fantasy.

vardax assumes Gaussian observation errors,y = H(x) + \varepsilon, \text{ with } \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, R)

where y \in \mathbb{R}^m are the observations and R is the observation-error covariance, so p(y \mid x) = \mathcal{N}(y; H(x), R). The observation cost in the variational problem is the negative log-likelihood up to a constant,J_\text{obs}(x) = \frac{1}{2} \|y - H(x)\|^2_{R^{-1}} = \frac{1}{2} (y - H(x))^\top R^{-1} (y - H(x))

Non-Gaussian likelihoods (Student-t, censored, count data) require
either a non-Gaussian extension of J_\text{obs} or amortized
inference with a flow / score-based head (chapter 10).

Every vardax observation operator satisfies
pipekit_cycle.ObservationOperator, restated here with typed signatures:

from typing import Protocol

import lineax as lx
from jaxtyping import Array, Float

# Shapes: N state cells; M observations


# today* (pipekit_cycle)
# the shipped protocol types both members as Any
class ObservationOperator(Protocol):
    # ŷ = H(x)
    def __call__(self, state: Float[Array, " n"]) -> Float[Array, " m"]:
        """Forward: H(x)."""

    # H′(x), the tangent-linear operator at x
    def linearize(self, state: Float[Array, " n"]) -> lx.AbstractLinearOperator:
        """Tangent-linear operator H'(x) for use in 4DVar inner loops."""

Program 2.1:Restates the observation-operator protocol: the forward map of 

(2.1) and its tangent linear.

The linearize() method returns a lineax.AbstractLinearOperator
(typically JacobianLinearOperator via autodiff, but structured
overrides are common). The transpose / adjoint comes for free from
lineax.

This contract is the same regardless of whether the operator is a
masked identity, an averaging kernel, or a multi-instrument fusion.

In the simplest case we observe the state where the mask is non-zero,H(x) = m \odot x, \text{ with } m \in \{0, 1\}^n

where \odot is the element-wise product.

Tangent-linear: H'(x) = \mathrm{diag}(m). Use case: SSH altimetry
along-track gaps, SST with cloud masks, in-situ samples on a grid.

The mask is passed per call, so the models apply it to H' themselves. The examples on this page build on each other, starting from a toy state on N = 6 cells.

import jax.numpy as jnp
import lineax as lx
import vardax as vdx

# Shapes: N = 6 state cells

# x, a toy state
state = jnp.linspace(1.0, 2.0, 6)  # (N,)
# m ∈ {0, 1}ᴺ, cells 2 and 5 unobserved
mask = jnp.array([1.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.0])  # (N,)

# today (vardax)
masked_obs = vdx.MaskedIdentity()
# H(x) = m ⊙ x
gappy_obs = masked_obs(state, mask=mask)  # (N,) → (N,)
print(gappy_obs)

Program 2.2:Computes the masked identity 

(2.3) on a toy state of six cells.

It prints [1.  1.2 0.  1.6 1.8 0. ].

A pre-computed projection from state to observation space isH(x) = H_\text{mat} \cdot x

where H_\text{mat} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n} is a fixed matrix.

Use case: Lagrangian footprint matrix from a particle simulator
(observation at receptor = footprint-weighted source field), spectral
filtering, spatial interpolation. The matrix is stored as an
AbstractLinearOperator so structure (sparse, low-rank, Kronecker) can
be exploited.

Here the footprint F = H_\text{mat} maps the six cells to M = 3 receptors, each averaging two neighbouring cells.

# Shapes: N = 6 state cells; M = 3 receptors

# (½ ½), the average of two neighbouring cells
pair_average = jnp.array([[0.5, 0.5]])  # (1, 2)
# F = I₃ ⊗ (½ ½), each receptor averages two neighbouring cells
footprint = jnp.kron(jnp.eye(3), pair_average)  # (M, N)
# today (lineax)
footprint_op = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(footprint)  # (M, N) op
# today (vardax)
footprint_obs = vdx.LinearObs(operator=footprint_op)
# H(x) = F x
receptor_obs = footprint_obs(state)  # (N,) → (M,)
print(receptor_obs)

Program 2.3:Computes the linear projection 

(2.4) through a footprint matrix of three receptors.

It prints [1.1 1.5 1.9].

For satellite L2 products derived from optimal-estimation retrievals
(TROPOMI CH₄, EMIT CH₄, OCO CO₂, MOPITT CO, …), the L2 retrieval is
not a direct sample of the mixing-ratio profile x. The retrieval
applies a smoothing matrix A (the averaging kernel) and falls back to
a retrieval prior x_a where the signal is weak:\hat{y} = A (h \odot x + (1 - h) \odot x_a)

where the symbols are

Symbol

Description

x \in \mathbb{R}^N

Model state (profile, surface field)

x_a \in \mathbb{R}^N

Retrieval prior from L2 metadata

h \in \mathbb{R}^N

Weighting vector (often pressure-weighted)

A \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}

Averaging kernel matrix

Tangent-linear: H'(x) = A \cdot \mathrm{diag}(h).

Skipping the averaging kernel is the most common cause of bias in
operational satellite inversions. Treating an L2 retrieval as a
direct measurement of the truth gives systematically wrong posteriors,
especially when the retrieval prior x_a differs from the inversion
prior x_b. vardax exposes AveragingKernel as a first-class operator
because this is a day-one requirement, not a future feature.

The toy kernel A below is tridiagonal, the prior x_a is flat and the sensitivity h falls from 1 to 0.2 with height. The check of the tangent linear against A \mathrm{diag}(h) formed densely prints True.

import einx

# Shapes: N = 6 levels

# the two nearest neighbours of each level
neighbours = jnp.eye(6, k=1) + jnp.eye(6, k=-1)  # (N, N)
# A = ½ I + ¼ neighbours, a tridiagonal smoothing kernel
kernel = 0.5 * jnp.eye(6) + 0.25 * neighbours  # (N, N)
# x_a, a flat retrieval prior
retrieval_prior = jnp.full(6, 1.8)  # (N,)
# h, sensitivity falling off with height
weighting_vector = jnp.linspace(1.0, 0.2, 6)  # (N,)
# today (lineax)
kernel_op = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(kernel)  # (N, N) op

# today (vardax)
averaging_kernel = vdx.AveragingKernel(
    kernel_matrix=kernel_op,
    prior_profile=retrieval_prior,
    pressure_weights=weighting_vector,
)
# ŷ = A (h ⊙ x + (1 − h) ⊙ x_a)
retrieved = averaging_kernel(state)  # (N,) → (N,)
# today (vardax)
# H′(x) = A diag(h)
kernel_tangent = averaging_kernel.linearize(state)  # (N, N) op
# A diag(h), formed densely to check
dense_tangent = einx.multiply("i j, j -> i j", kernel, weighting_vector)  # (N, N)
print(bool(jnp.allclose(kernel_tangent.as_matrix(), dense_tangent)))

Program 2.4:Computes the averaging-kernel operator 

(2.5) and checks its tangent linear against the dense A diag(h).

When A has structure (Kronecker for separable kernels, low-rank for
under-determined inversions, banded for compactly-supported kernels),
store it as a gaussx.AbstractLinearOperator. The tangent linear
A \cdot \mathrm{diag}(h) is then computed without ever materialising
the dense A.

Operational satellite work combines multiple instruments. Each instrument has its own H_i, mask m_i, error covariance R_i and optionally an averaging kernel (A_i, x_{a,i}, h_i). The fused observation cost composes 

(2.2) at the likelihood level,J_\text{obs}(x) = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \alpha_i \cdot \frac{1}{2} \|m_i \odot (y_i - H_i(x))\|^2_{R_i^{-1}}

where \mathcal{I} is the set of instruments and \alpha_i is a per-instrument weight. The weight defaults to uniform; tuning it is for hierarchical bias correction (Epic 9). Each InstrumentSpec carries its own operator, mask and R_i. Quality masks zero-weight unreliable pixels, so they contribute zero log-likelihood rather than being dropped, which lets us audit the effective per-instrument observation count.

The registry below reuses the three operators above: TROPOMI through the averaging kernel, EMIT through the masked identity and GHGSat through the footprint. It evaluates each H_i(x) but does not form the cost itself.

import jax

# Shapes: N = 6 state cells; M = 3 receptors

state_structure = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((6,), jnp.float32)
receptor_structure = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((3,), jnp.float32)
# today (lineax)
state_identity = lx.IdentityLinearOperator(state_structure)  # (N, N) op
# today (lineax)
receptor_identity = lx.IdentityLinearOperator(receptor_structure)  # (M, M) op
# R_TROPOMI = 0.04 I
tropomi_cov = 0.04 * state_identity  # (N, N) op
# R_EMIT = 0.01 I
emit_cov = 0.01 * state_identity  # (N, N) op
# R_GHGSat = 0.0025 I
ghgsat_cov = 0.0025 * receptor_identity  # (M, M) op

# today (vardax)
registry = vdx.InstrumentRegistry(
    entries={
        "TROPOMI": vdx.InstrumentSpec(
            obs_op=averaging_kernel,
            mask=jnp.ones(6),
            obs_cov_op=tropomi_cov,
            instrument_id="TROPOMI",
        ),
        "EMIT": vdx.InstrumentSpec(
            obs_op=masked_obs,
            mask=mask,
            obs_cov_op=emit_cov,
            instrument_id="EMIT",
        ),
        "GHGSat": vdx.InstrumentSpec(
            obs_op=footprint_obs,
            mask=jnp.ones(3),
            obs_cov_op=ghgsat_cov,
            instrument_id="GHGSat",
        ),
    }
)
# today (vardax)
fusion = vdx.MultiInstrumentFusion(registry=registry)
# {i: Hᵢ(x)}
predicted = fusion(state)  # (N,) → {i: (Mᵢ,)}
# today (vardax)
stacked_op = fusion.to_observation_operator()
# [H_EMIT(x); H_GHGSat(x); H_TROPOMI(x)], in sorted id order
stacked = stacked_op(state)  # (N,) → (N + M + N,)
print({name: obs.shape for name, obs in predicted.items()}, stacked.shape)

Program 2.5:Evaluates each instrument operator of the fusion cost 

(2.6) through a registry of three instruments.

It prints {'TROPOMI': (6,), 'EMIT': (6,), 'GHGSat': (3,)} (15,).

MultiInstrumentFusion.__call__ returns dict[str, Array] (per-instrument predicted observations), and MultiInstrumentFusion.cost sums the weighted per-instrument terms. For strict pipekit_cycle.ObservationOperator contexts, the .to_observation_operator() adapter flattens to a single concatenated output, and its linearize is the Jacobian of that map, the per-instrument H_i' stacked row-wise. Pass fusion.obs_cov_op() as the model’s R with that adapter: its blocks are R_i / \alpha_i, so the model minimises the same weighted cost.

When the control is not the state but a source, a forcing or a parameter vector q, the observation operator is a downstream model run \mathcal{G}(q): a transport model followed by its receptors, a radiative-transfer forward, a neural emulator. The cost J(q) is then exactly the 3DVar cost 

(5.1) with x = q, x_b = q_b and H = \mathcal{G}, or OI (chapter 4) when \mathcal{G} is linear. CallableObs wraps any differentiable JAX function as that operator; linearize(x) is a matrix-free lineax.JacobianLinearOperator, so the tangent-linear map is a JVP and its adjoint a VJP.

In the example below the control is P = 3 unconstrained emission parameters q, and \mathcal{G}(q) = G \operatorname{softplus}(q) maps them to M = 6 receptors through a transport matrix G that decays with the distance between receptor and source. The observations are noise-free, B = I and R = 10^{-2} I.

import optimistix as optx

# Shapes: S = 1 sample; T = 1 time; P = 3 sources; M = 6 receptors

# G, receptor m sees source p with weight exp(−|m − 2p|)
receptor_index = jnp.arange(6.0)  # (M,)
source_index = 2.0 * jnp.arange(3.0)  # (P,)
offset = einx.subtract("m, p -> m p", receptor_index, source_index)  # (M, P)
# |m − 2p|
distance = jnp.abs(offset)  # (M, P)
# G = exp(−|m − 2p|)
transport = jnp.exp(-distance)  # (M, P)


# user
def run_model(source: Float[Array, "t p"]) -> Float[Array, "t m"]:
    # e = log(1 + exp(q)), positive emission rates
    emission = jax.nn.softplus(source)  # (T, P)
    # 𝒢(q) = G softplus(q)
    return einx.dot("t p, m p -> t m", emission, transport)  # (T, M)


# q_b = 0, q_true = (0.5, −0.3, 0.2)
source_background = jnp.zeros((1, 3))  # (T, P)
true_source = jnp.array([[0.5, -0.3, 0.2]])  # (T, P)
# y = 𝒢(q_true), noise-free
receptor_data = run_model(true_source)  # (T, M)

source_structure = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((1, 3), jnp.float32)
receptor_data_structure = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((1, 6), jnp.float32)
# today (lineax)
# B = I
source_cov = lx.IdentityLinearOperator(source_structure)  # (T P, T P) op
# today (lineax)
receptor_data_identity = lx.IdentityLinearOperator(receptor_data_structure)
# today (lineax)
# R = 10⁻² I; tagged PSD so the default CG solve accepts it
receptor_cov = lx.TaggedLinearOperator(  # (T M, T M) op
    1e-2 * receptor_data_identity, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
)
# today (vardax)
# H(q) = 𝒢(q)
model_obs = vdx.CallableObs(fn=run_model)
# today (vardax)
# J(q) = ½ ‖q − q_b‖²_{B⁻¹} + ½ ‖y − 𝒢(q)‖²_{R⁻¹}
parameter_3dvar = vdx.ThreeDVar(
    obs_op=model_obs,
    prior_mean=source_background,
    prior_cov_op=source_cov,
    obs_cov_op=receptor_cov,
    minimiser=optx.BFGS(rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-6),
)
# today (vardax)
receptor_batch = vdx.Batch1D(
    input=einx.id("t m -> 1 t m", receptor_data),  # (T, M) → (S, T, M)
    mask=jnp.ones((1, 1, 6)),
)
# q* = argmin_q J(q)
source_analysis = parameter_3dvar(receptor_batch)  # → (S, T, P)
print(source_analysis[0])

Program 2.6:Minimises the 3DVar cost 

(5.1) over emission parameters q, with a transport model as the observation operator.

It prints [[ 0.4838582  -0.27665472  0.19014639]], close to q_\text{true} = (0.5, -0.3, 0.2); the prior pulls each rate slightly towards q_b = 0.

The observation shape need not match the state shape. Prefer
LinearObs when you already hold an explicit or structured matrix you
want to reuse.

For a model that defines only a reverse-mode rule (a jax.custom_vjp),
pass CallableObs(fn=..., jac="bwd"): forward-mode linearisation raises
on those as soon as an analysis or a posterior needs H'. Matrix-free,
lineax then applies H'v by transposing the VJP, which fails when the
backward pass holds a loop JAX cannot transpose. A diffrax solve is
the common case: RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint runs a while_loop. Add
materialise=True and linearize forms the Jacobian once, with one VJP
per observation; that is cheap when the control is small, as a source or
parameter vector usually is. The toy simulate below integrates dc/dt = q - c to t = 1, so H'(q) = (1 - e^{-1}) I, and the block prints True:

import diffrax as dfx

# Shapes: T = 1 time; P = 3 sources


# user
def simulate(source: Float[Array, "t p"]) -> Float[Array, "t p"]:
    # today (diffrax)
    # dc/dt = q − c
    term = dfx.ODETerm(lambda time, conc, rate: rate - conc)
    # today (diffrax)
    # c(1) from c(0) = 0, reverse mode by RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint
    solution = dfx.diffeqsolve(
        term,
        dfx.Tsit5(),
        t0=0.0,
        t1=1.0,
        dt0=0.1,
        y0=jnp.zeros_like(source),
        args=source,
    )
    return solution.ys[-1]  # (T, P)


# today (vardax)
simulator_obs = vdx.CallableObs(fn=simulate, jac="bwd", materialise=True)
# today (vardax)
# H′(q) = ∂c(1)/∂q = (1 − e⁻¹) I
simulator_tangent = simulator_obs.linearize(true_source)  # (T P, T P) op
# (1 − e⁻¹) I, the exact tangent
exact_tangent = (1.0 - jnp.exp(-1.0)) * jnp.eye(3)  # (T P, T P)
print(bool(jnp.allclose(simulator_tangent.as_matrix(), exact_tangent, atol=1e-4)))

Program 2.7:Materialises the tangent linear of a diffrax-solve observation operator 

(2.1) with one VJP per observation.

For incremental 4DVar (chapter 8), every observation operator must expose linearize, whose operator applies H' with mv and H'^\top with transpose().mv. The pair must pass the adjoint test\langle H' u, v \rangle = \langle u, (H')^\top v \rangle \text{ for all } u, v

up to floating-point tolerance, where u is a state-space vector and v an observation-space vector. Failing this test means the gradient flowing back through H is wrong, and any downstream optimiser will take wrong steps. The block below draws random u = \delta x and v = r and prints True; tests/test_obs_operators.py runs the same test for AveragingKernel.

# Shapes: N = 6 levels

key = jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
key_tangent, key_residual = jax.random.split(key)

# δx ~ 𝒩(0, I)
increment = jax.random.normal(key_tangent, (6,))  # (N,)
# r ~ 𝒩(0, I)
residual = jax.random.normal(key_residual, (6,))  # (N,)

# today (vardax)
# H′(x)
kernel_tangent = averaging_kernel.linearize(state)  # (N, N) op
# H′ δx, the forward tangent-linear model
tangent_increment = kernel_tangent.mv(increment)  # (N,) → (N,)
# H′ᵀ r, the adjoint
adjoint_residual = kernel_tangent.transpose().mv(residual)  # (N,) → (N,)
# ⟨H′ δx, r⟩
forward_inner = einx.dot("n, n ->", tangent_increment, residual)  # → ()
# ⟨δx, H′ᵀ r⟩
adjoint_inner = einx.dot("n, n ->", increment, adjoint_residual)  # → ()
print(bool(jnp.isclose(forward_inner, adjoint_inner, atol=1e-5)))

Program 2.8:Checks the adjoint test 

(2.7) for the averaging kernel.

R is supplied as a lineax.AbstractLinearOperator. Common
parameterisations:

Diagonal: lineax.DiagonalLinearOperator(variances). The default for heteroscedastic retrievals (per-pixel σ from L2 metadata).

Block-diagonal: gaussx.BlockDiag(*instrument_covs). Per-instrument diagonals when fusing.

Structured: kernellib.ImplicitKernelOperator(matern, coords) if observation errors are spatially correlated (rare, but it matters for high-resolution imaging spectrometers).

The models’ solves reject gaussx operators until they are wrapped as a lx.FunctionLinearOperator, as 

chapter 4 does for B.

The choice flows into 

(2.2) via R^{-1}, which is applied lazily: the inverse is never materialised, only applied to vectors via lineax.CG.

hierarchy.lvl2: When the observation model is wrong
When the observation model is wrong

records.content:
A common failure mode: H is misspecified (wrong averaging kernel,
missing instrument bias, ignored representation error). The MAP
x^* then converges to a wrong answer with a confident-looking
posterior. Diagnostics:

Innovation statistics d = y - H(x_b). Should be roughly mean-zero
and consistent with \sqrt{\mathrm{diag}(H B H^\top + R)}. Large
systematic offsets indicate bias.

Posterior vs prior log-evidence ratio. If the data move the
posterior much further than \sigma_\text{post} from the prior, the
B or R assumptions are wrong.

Cross-instrument disagreement. Per-instrument residual statistics
should be consistent; large disagreements flag uncorrected bias.

Epic 9 adds joint bias estimation for the cross-instrument case.

design/api/observation_operators.md

For 4D analysis, observations y_t at times t = 0, 1, \ldots, T must be connected to the initial state x_0 through the rollout 

(1.3), where M_t propagates the state forward from time 0 to time t. The dynamics enter the cost as the composition H_t \circ M_t.

vardax does not own dynamics; those come from somax (geophysical fluids), plumax (atmospheric transport and methane) or any user code. What vardax owns is the interface to dynamics (the pipekit_cycle.ForwardModel protocol) and the adjoint composition (delegated to diffrax.AbstractAdjoint).

A forward supplies step(state, dt), a default dt and a state_signature. The Lorenz-63 model below, with state s = (x, y, z) and the vector field f of 

(15.1), advances by forward Euler steps and satisfies the protocol structurally, and the check prints True; the later blocks on this page build on it.

import equinox as eqx
import jax.numpy as jnp
import pipekit_cycle as pc
from jaxtyping import Array, Float

# Shapes: N = 3 state components


# user
class Lorenz63(eqx.Module):
    """Lorenz-63 dynamics, advanced by forward Euler steps."""

    sigma: float = 10.0
    rho: float = 28.0
    beta: float = 8.0 / 3.0
    dt: float = 0.01

    def vector_field(self, state: Float[Array, " n"]) -> Float[Array, " n"]:
        x, y, z = state
        # f(s) = (σ (y − x), x (ρ − z) − y, x y − β z)
        return jnp.stack(
            [self.sigma * (y - x), x * (self.rho - z) - y, x * y - self.beta * z]
        )

    def step(self, state: Float[Array, " n"], dt: float) -> Float[Array, " n"]:
        """Advance state by dt."""
        # sₖ₊₁ = sₖ + Δt f(sₖ)
        return state + dt * self.vector_field(state)

    @property
    def state_signature(self) -> None:
        return None


dynamics = Lorenz63()
# today (pipekit_cycle)
print(isinstance(dynamics, pc.ForwardModel))

Program 3.1:Defines Lorenz-63 

(15.1) as a forward-Euler forward model and checks that it satisfies the protocol.

somax.ShallowWaterModel, plumax.GaussianPlumeForward, and
user-defined dynamics all satisfy this protocol natively. From vardax’s
perspective they’re interchangeable.

For multi-step rollouts, vardax composes step calls into a trajectory with a lax.scan; a forward that is an ODE integrates each step with diffrax.diffeqsolve itself. The choice of ODE integrator
(Tsit5, Dopri5, Heun, …) is on the dynamics, not on vardax.

The strong-constraint 4DVar cost 

(6.1) sums an observation term over every time. Minimising it over x_0 requires the gradient 

(6.2), which by the chain rule pulls each weighted residual H'_t{}^\top R_t^{-1} (H_t(M_t(x_0)) - y_t) back to the initial time through (M'_t)^\top, where M'_t and H'_t are the tangent-linear dynamics and observation operator.

The transpose (M'_t)^\top is the adjoint model, which was historically hand-coded line by line (Talagrand and Courtier 1987, Errico 1997). Modern numerical libraries make this far less painful: diffrax provides the adjoint of any diffeqsolve call automatically, in several flavours.

vardax exposes forward_adjoint: diffrax.AbstractAdjoint as a
constructor slot on StrongFourDVar, WeakFourDVar,
IncrementalFourDVar and ReducedBasisFourDVar. It reaches diffrax
through the forward: the model calls forward.with_adjoint(adjoint)
(the 

SupportsForwardAdjoint protocol) and rolls
out the forward it returns. A per-step forward has no integrator to hand
the adjoint to, so passing forward_adjoint= with one raises
ValueError; bound its memory with checkpoint= instead (below).

Default: RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint. Standard autodiff with recursive checkpointing, which balances memory and recompute. It supports reverse mode only, so as_forward_model(dt) differentiates each one-step solve with DirectAdjoint instead, which IncrementalFourDVar’s forward-mode tangent-linear model needs; pass as_forward_model(dt, adjoint=...) to choose another.

For long assimilation windows: BacksolveAdjoint. Solves the continuous adjoint ODE 

(12.1) backwards in time, with constant memory in the forward-trajectory length. Caveat: the reverse-time ODE may be stiff even when the forward ODE is not (diffusion-dominated problems, for example). If forward uses Tsit5, backward should typically use the same, and if the reverse problem is stiff, switch to an implicit solver; the diffrax docs list stable integrators.

For parameter estimation: ForwardMode. When you’re sensitive to a
small number of parameters (e.g. a single emission rate Q in a
methane Tier I problem), forward sensitivity is cheaper than reverse.

For debugging: DirectAdjoint. Plain reverse mode through the lax.scan of forward steps, slow but transparent. Its O(K) memory is fine for K = 10 steps but painful for K = 1000, so it is the wrong choice for long windows.

If M_t is linear, the tangent-linear model 

(8.1) is just M_t itself (no linearisation needed). For IncrementalFourDVar and operational 4DVar, the inner loop is in this situation: the outer nonlinear model is wrapped, but the inner loop operates on its tangent linear, computed once per outer iteration via jax.linearize and reused across many CG iterations.

The block below linearises at x_b = (1, 1, 1), pulls back a cotangent r and prints True.

import einx
import jax
import lineax as lx

# Shapes: N = 3 state components

state_structure = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((3,), jnp.float32)
# x_b, the outer iterate
background = jnp.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0])  # (N,)
# r, a cotangent to pull back
cotangent = jnp.array([1.0, -1.0, 0.5])  # (N,)


# user
def one_step(state: Float[Array, " n"]) -> Float[Array, " n"]:
    # M(s) = s + Δt f(s)
    return dynamics.step(state, dynamics.dt)  # (N,)


# today (jax)
# δx ↦ M′(x_b) δx, the tangent-linear step
_, tangent_step = jax.linearize(one_step, background)
# today (lineax)
# M′ as an operator, so lineax derives M′ᵀ
tangent_op = lx.FunctionLinearOperator(tangent_step, state_structure)  # (N, N) op
# today (lineax)
adjoint_op = tangent_op.transpose()  # (N, N) op
# M′ᵀ r, the adjoint step
adjoint_step = adjoint_op.mv(cotangent)  # (N,) → (N,)
# today (jax)
jacobian_fn = jax.jacfwd(one_step)
# M′(x_b), formed densely to check
step_jacobian = jacobian_fn(background)  # (N,) → (N, N)
# M′ᵀ r = Σᵢ M′ᵢⱼ rᵢ
expected_adjoint = einx.dot("i j, i -> j", step_jacobian, cotangent)  # (N,)
print(bool(jnp.allclose(adjoint_step, expected_adjoint)))

Program 3.2:Linearises one Lorenz-63 step as in 

(8.1) and checks the lineax adjoint step against the dense Jacobian.

For the unwrapped StrongFourDVar and WeakFourDVar, the full
nonlinear M_t is integrated each outer step and diffrax’s adjoint
handles the gradient computation.

For SDEs (Langevin dynamics in Lagrangian transport, stochastic parameterisations), diffrax still applies: diffeqsolve handles SDE integration via EulerMaruyama, Heun, etc., and the adjoint methods work in the SDE setting too (with caveats around non-deterministic reverse integration).

vardax does not currently expose dedicated SDE-DA classes; the existing
4DVar variants work as long as the SDE realisations are seeded
deterministically (e.g. via a jax.random.PRNGKey carried through the
batch).

For typical 4DVar with between T = 10 and T = 100 assimilation cycles and a shallow-water ForwardModel, the rollout 

(1.3) is one diffeqsolve saved at every step. The toy below rolls Lorenz-63 out for K = 100 steps of \Delta t = 0.01 and differentiates \frac{1}{2} \|s(t_K)\|^2, the squared norm of the final state, with two adjoints; it continues the block above.

import diffrax as dfx

# Shapes: K = 100 steps; N = 3 state components


# user
def rollout(
    initial_state: Float[Array, " n"],
    forward: Lorenz63,
    n_steps: int,
    dt: float,
    *,
    adjoint: dfx.AbstractAdjoint,
) -> Float[Array, "k n"]:
    """Integrate forward and return the trajectory."""
    # today (diffrax)
    # ds/dt = f(s)
    term = dfx.ODETerm(lambda time, state, args: forward.vector_field(state))
    # tₖ = k Δt, k = 0, …, K
    save_times = dt * jnp.arange(n_steps + 1)  # (K + 1,)
    # today (diffrax)
    # s(tₖ) = s₀ + ∫₀^{tₖ} f(s) dt
    solution = dfx.diffeqsolve(
        term,
        dfx.Tsit5(),
        t0=0.0,
        t1=n_steps * dt,
        dt0=dt,
        y0=initial_state,
        saveat=dfx.SaveAt(ts=save_times),
        adjoint=adjoint,
    )
    return solution.ys  # (K + 1, N)


# user
def final_state_cost(
    initial_state: Float[Array, " n"], adjoint: dfx.AbstractAdjoint
) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    # user
    # s(tₖ) = Mₖ(s₀), k = 0, …, K
    trajectory = rollout(initial_state, dynamics, 100, 0.01, adjoint=adjoint)
    # s(t_K)
    final_state = trajectory[-1]  # (N,)
    # ½ ‖s(t_K)‖²
    return 0.5 * einx.dot("n, n ->", final_state, final_state)  # → ()


# today (jax)
cost_grad = jax.grad(final_state_cost)
# today (diffrax)
# ∇ₛ₀ by discretise-then-optimise, with recursive checkpoints
checkpoint_grad = cost_grad(background, dfx.RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint())  # (N,)
# today (diffrax)
# ∇ₛ₀ by optimise-then-discretise, solving the adjoint ODE backwards
backsolve_grad = cost_grad(background, dfx.BacksolveAdjoint())  # (N,)
print(bool(jnp.allclose(checkpoint_grad, backsolve_grad, rtol=1e-2)))

Program 3.3:Differentiates the rollout 

(1.3) through the discrete adjoint and through the adjoint ODE 

(12.1).

It prints True. The two gradients differ by about 0.1%, because BacksolveAdjoint discretises the continuous adjoint ODE while RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint differentiates the discrete solve exactly.

Inside vardax, the rollout is composed inside the cost function. Give the forward a with_adjoint method that stores the adjoint and passes it to diffeqsolve; the model’s forward_adjoint slot then calls it, so that when jax.grad(J)(x_0) is called, the gradient flows back through the chosen adjoint path.

With H_t the identity, StrongFourDVar recovers the initial state x_\text{true} = (1.2, 0.8, 1.1) from a noise-free window of T = 5 times, starting from x_b, once with the forward’s own adjoint and once with forward_adjoint=dfx.BacksolveAdjoint():

import dataclasses
from collections.abc import Callable

import vardax as vdx

# Shapes: S = 1 window; T = 5 times; N = 3 state components


# user
@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True)
class DiffraxForward:
    vector_field: Callable[[Float[Array, " n"]], Float[Array, " n"]]
    dt: float
    adjoint: dfx.AbstractAdjoint = dfx.RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint()

    def step(self, state: Float[Array, " n"], dt: float) -> Float[Array, " n"]:
        # today (diffrax)
        # ds/dt = f(s)
        term = dfx.ODETerm(lambda time, state, args: self.vector_field(state))
        # today (diffrax)
        # s(t + Δt) = s(t) + ∫ f(s) dt over one step
        solution = dfx.diffeqsolve(
            term,
            dfx.Tsit5(),
            t0=0.0,
            t1=dt,
            dt0=dt,
            y0=state,
            adjoint=self.adjoint,
        )
        return solution.ys[-1]  # (N,)

    def with_adjoint(self, adjoint: dfx.AbstractAdjoint) -> "DiffraxForward":
        return dataclasses.replace(self, adjoint=adjoint)


forward = DiffraxForward(vector_field=dynamics.vector_field, dt=0.01)
# x_true(t₀), the initial state to recover
true_initial = jnp.array([1.2, 0.8, 1.1])  # (N,)
# user
# yₜ = Mₜ(x_true), observed everywhere without noise
window_obs = rollout(  # (N,) → (T, N)
    true_initial, dynamics, 4, 0.01, adjoint=dfx.RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint()
)
# today (lineax)
# B = I
prior_cov = lx.IdentityLinearOperator(state_structure)  # (N, N) op
# today (lineax)
# R = σ² I, σ = 0.1; tagged PSD so the default CG solve accepts it
obs_cov = lx.TaggedLinearOperator(  # (N, N) op
    0.01 * prior_cov, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
)
# today (vardax)
window = vdx.Batch1D(
    input=einx.id("t n -> 1 t n", window_obs),  # (T, N) → (S, T, N)
    mask=jnp.ones((1, 5, 3)),
)

# today (vardax)
# J(x₀) = ½ ‖x₀ − x_b‖²_{B⁻¹} + ½ Σₜ ‖yₜ − Mₜ(x₀)‖²_{R⁻¹}
default_4dvar = vdx.StrongFourDVar(
    forward=forward,
    obs_op=vdx.MaskedIdentity(),
    prior_mean=background,
    prior_cov_op=prior_cov,
    obs_cov_op=obs_cov,
)
# today (vardax)
# the same cost, differentiated through the adjoint ODE
backsolve_4dvar = vdx.StrongFourDVar(
    forward=forward,
    obs_op=vdx.MaskedIdentity(),
    prior_mean=background,
    prior_cov_op=prior_cov,
    obs_cov_op=obs_cov,
    forward_adjoint=dfx.BacksolveAdjoint(),
)
# x₀* = argmin J(x₀)
default_analysis = default_4dvar(window)  # → (S, N)
# x₀* again, through the adjoint ODE
backsolve_analysis = backsolve_4dvar(window)  # → (S, N)

print(default_analysis[0], backsolve_analysis[0])
print(bool(jnp.allclose(default_analysis, backsolve_analysis, atol=1e-3)))

Program 3.4:Minimises the strong-constraint cost 

(6.1) with two forward adjoints and compares the analyses.

Both analyses print [1.199159  0.8008326 1.0997877], and the check prints True: the adjoint changes how the gradient is computed, not the analysis.

Most forwards are a single step(x, dt) (an RK4 step of a finite-volume
model, a learned emulator). Reverse mode through a lax.scan of such
steps stores every intermediate of every step. The 4DVar models’
checkpoint= slot wraps blocks of steps in jax.checkpoint, so the
backward pass recomputes them instead: True checkpoints every step, an
integer k every block of k steps. The gradient is unchanged.

On Lorenz-96 (N = 40, RK4, 500 steps, float64, CPU) the compiled
gradient’s temporary memory drops from 1.61 MB to 0.49 MB with
checkpoint=True and to 0.37 MB with checkpoint=10. What remains is
mostly the trajectory itself, which the observation cost reads at every
time.

Vectorise over the batch dimension, not the time dimension. Time
is intrinsically sequential; batch is embarrassingly parallel. Use
eqx.filter_vmap over the batch axis.

Checkpoint sparingly with RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint. The default
number of checkpoints (int(log2(n_steps)) + 1) is usually right.
Override only if profiling shows memory pressure.

For linear-Gaussian state estimation, the posterior is Gaussian in
closed form and the analysis is a single matrix expression. This is
the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE), known in geosciences as
Optimal Interpolation (OI). It is the first method you should reach
for when the regime allows it (Decision D16).

The Kalman gain in 

(4.4) requires inverting an m \times m matrix (observation-space form). The second form of 

(4.5) instead inverts the posterior precision B^{-1} + H^\top R^{-1} H, an n \times n matrix (state-space form).

Pick the form whose matrix is smaller:

Regime

Form

Inversion size

m \ll n (sparse observations)

Kalman gain K of 

(4.4)

m \times m

m \gg n (dense observations)

precision (P^*)^{-1} of 

(4.5)

n \times n

For SSH altimetry with sparse along-track samples and a 2D grid, m \ll n and the observation-space form wins. For a satellite imager with one observation per state cell, m \approx n and either works.

OptimalInterpolation solves the observation-space system (H B H^\top + R) v = y - H x_b by default, and the state-space system (B^{-1} + H^\top R^{-1} H) \delta x = H^\top R^{-1} (y - H x_b) with form="state". The block below fuses m = 2000 pixels into n = 3 unknowns and prints True: both forms give the same analysis.

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import lineax as lx
import vardax as vdx

# Shapes: n = 3 unknowns; m = 2000 pixels

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
key_design, key_obs = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(0))
# H, a dense design
design = jax.random.normal(key_design, (2000, 3))  # (M, N)
# y ~ 𝒩(0, I)
pixels = jax.random.normal(key_obs, (1, 2000))  # (S, M)
analyses = {}
for form in ("observation", "state"):
    # today (vardax)
    oi = vdx.OptimalInterpolation(
        obs_op=vdx.LinearObs(operator=lx.MatrixLinearOperator(design)),
        prior_mean=jnp.zeros(3),
        # B = I
        prior_cov_op=lx.IdentityLinearOperator(jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((3,), jnp.float64)),
        # R = 10⁻² I
        obs_cov_op=lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(jnp.full(2000, 1e-2)),
        solver=lx.Cholesky(),
        form=form,
    )
    # x* = x_b + δx
    analyses[form] = oi(vdx.Batch1D(input=pixels, mask=jnp.ones_like(pixels)))  # (S, M) → (S, N)
print(bool(jnp.allclose(analyses["observation"], analyses["state"], rtol=1e-8)))

Solves one BLUE in the observation-space and the state-space form and checks they agree.

The observation-space solve factors a 2000 \times 2000 matrix here, the state-space one a 3 \times 3 matrix.

records.content:
Both forms require solving a linear system, not inverting a matrix
explicitly. kernellib and gaussx supply structured operators:

B as a Matérn covariance: kernellib.ImplicitKernelOperator(matern, coords) applies it matrix-free with O(N) memory, and gaussx.Kronecker exploits separable grids. Both can be passed to a vardax model directly when the state is a single (N,) vector; for a (T, N) state, wrap the mat-vec as lx.FunctionLinearOperator(apply, structure, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag), as the example below does.

R as lineax.DiagonalLinearOperator(variances), which is diagonal and trivial.

H B H^\top is never materialised; only v \mapsto H B H^\top v is needed, which is one mat-vec each with H^\top, B and H.

The innovation system (H B H^\top + R) v = y - H x_b is then solved by lineax.CG, returning v in O(k \cdot m) time where k is the CG iteration count (typically tens). The analysis 

(4.4) is then x^* = x_b + B H^\top v, one more mat-vec.

CG runs at a fixed tolerance with a step cap, so its analysis is
approximate, and an ill-conditioned H B H^\top + R (small R, smooth
B) can exhaust the cap. When the innovation system is small enough to
factor, pass a direct solver instead:
OptimalInterpolation(..., solver=lx.Cholesky()) (or
lx.AutoLinearSolver(well_posed=True)) gives the BLUE to machine
precision, and posterior() then uses the same solver for its
covariance.

A full OI on a 2D Matérn prior with 50,000 grid cells and 5,000
observations takes seconds on a single GPU. No materialised matrices,
no O(n^3) factorisations.

The example is a toy along-track problem: N = 20 cells every 10 km on one track, M = 5 samples, a Matérn-3/2 prior B with length scale \ell = 50 km and standard deviation \sigma_b = 0.1 m around a zero climatology, and R = \sigma_o^2 I with \sigma_o = 0.02 m. The truth is a smooth sine wave and the observations add noise to it. The state has shape (T, N) with T = 1, as posterior expects.

import einx
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import kernellib as kl
import lineax as lx
import vardax as vdx
from jaxtyping import Array, Float

# Shapes: S = 1 sample; T = 1 time; N = 20 grid cells; M = 5 along-track samples
# D = 1 coordinate

key_noise = jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
# ℓ = 50 km, σ_b = 0.1 m, σ_o = 0.02 m
length_scale, prior_std, obs_std = 50.0, 0.1, 0.02
state_structure = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((1, 20), jnp.float32)


# user
def matern32(cell: Float[Array, " d"], other: Float[Array, " d"]) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    # (sᵢ − sⱼ)²
    squared_difference = (cell - other) ** 2  # (D,)
    # ‖sᵢ − sⱼ‖², with a floor so the gradient at r = 0 is finite
    squared_gap = einx.sum("d -> ", squared_difference) + 1e-12  # → ()
    # √3 r, with r = ‖sᵢ − sⱼ‖ / ℓ
    scaled_gap = jnp.sqrt(3.0 * squared_gap) / length_scale  # → ()
    # k(r) = σ_b² (1 + √3 r) exp(−√3 r)
    return prior_std**2 * (1.0 + scaled_gap) * jnp.exp(-scaled_gap)  # → ()


# user
def sample_track(state: Float[Array, "t n"]) -> Float[Array, "t m"]:
    # H x, the cells under the along-track samples
    return einx.dot("t n, m n -> t m", state, along_track)  # (T, M)


# user
def apply_prior_cov(state: Float[Array, "t n"]) -> Float[Array, "t n"]:
    # B xₜ at each time
    return jax.vmap(kernel_op.mv)(state)  # (T, N)


# sᵢ, cell centres every 10 km along one track
positions = jnp.linspace(0.0, 190.0, 20)  # (N,)
coords = einx.id("n -> n 1", positions)  # (N,) → (N, D)
# rows of I at the sampled cells
along_track = jnp.eye(20)[jnp.array([1, 5, 9, 13, 17])]  # (M, N)

# today (kernellib)
# B = [k(sᵢ, sⱼ)]ᵢⱼ, never materialised
kernel_op = kl.ImplicitKernelOperator(matern32, coords)  # (N, N) op
# today (lineax)
# B on (T, N) states, applied at each time
prior_cov = lx.FunctionLinearOperator(  # (T N, T N) PSD op
    apply_prior_cov, state_structure, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
)
# today (lineax)
along_track_op = lx.FunctionLinearOperator(  # (T M, T N) op
    sample_track, state_structure
)
# σ_o², one per sample
obs_var = jnp.full((1, 5), obs_std**2)  # (T, M)
# today (lineax)
# R = σ_o² I
obs_cov = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(obs_var)  # (T M, T M) op

# x_b = 0, a climatology
climatology_ssh = jnp.zeros((1, 20))  # (T, N)
# sᵢ laid out as a state
track_position = einx.id("n 1 -> 1 n", coords)  # (N, 1) → (T, N)
# x_true(s) = σ_b sin(2π s / 200 km), a smooth truth
truth = prior_std * jnp.sin(2.0 * jnp.pi * track_position / 200.0)  # (T, N)
# y = H x_true + σ_o ε, ε ~ 𝒩(0, I)
noise = obs_std * jax.random.normal(key_noise, (1, 5))  # (T, M)
# user
# H x_true
track_truth = sample_track(truth)  # (T, N) → (T, M)
obs = track_truth + noise  # (T, M)

# today (vardax)
# H x, a linear observation operator
along_track_obs = vdx.LinearObs(operator=along_track_op)
# today (vardax)
model = vdx.OptimalInterpolation(
    obs_op=along_track_obs,
    prior_mean=climatology_ssh,
    prior_cov_op=prior_cov,
    obs_cov_op=obs_cov,
    solver=lx.Cholesky(),
)
# today (vardax)
batch = vdx.Batch1D(
    input=einx.id("t m -> 1 t m", obs),  # (T, M) → (S, T, M)
    mask=jnp.ones((1, 1, 5)),
)
# x* = x_b + B Hᵀ (H B Hᵀ + R)⁻¹ (y − H x_b), one pass, no iteration
x_star = model(batch)  # → (S, T, N)

# today (vardax)
# P* = (B⁻¹ + Hᵀ R⁻¹ H)⁻¹, a lazy operator
posterior = model.posterior(batch)
# eᵢ at an observed cell (i = 1) and between samples (i = 3)
observed_cell = jnp.eye(20)[jnp.array([1])]  # (T, N)
gap_cell = jnp.eye(20)[jnp.array([3])]  # (T, N)
# P* eᵢ, one matrix-free product each
observed_column = posterior.cov.mv(observed_cell)  # (T, N) → (T, N)
gap_column = posterior.cov.mv(gap_cell)  # (T, N) → (T, N)
# σᵢ² = eᵢᵀ P* eᵢ
observed_var = einx.dot("t n, t n ->", observed_cell, observed_column)  # → ()
gap_var = einx.dot("t n, t n ->", gap_cell, gap_column)  # → ()

# ‖x_b − x_true‖
background_error = jnp.linalg.norm(climatology_ssh - truth)  # → ()
# ‖x* − x_true‖
analysis_error = jnp.linalg.norm(x_star[0] - truth)  # → ()
print(f"background error {background_error:.3f}, analysis error {analysis_error:.3f}")
print(f"posterior std {observed_var**0.5:.3f} observed, {gap_var**0.5:.3f} in a gap")

Program 4.2:Computes the OI analysis 

(4.4) and posterior covariance 

(4.5) of a toy along-track problem and reads two marginal standard deviations off P*.

It prints background error 0.316, analysis error 0.095 and posterior std 0.019 observed, 0.035 in a gap. The Cholesky solver makes the analysis and the posterior exact; the posterior solves the same innovation system as the analysis and never applies B^{-1}.

The posterior.cov is an AbstractLinearOperator representing P^*.
Sampling from the posterior is a mat-vec in (P^*)^{1/2}; the diagonal
of P^* (marginal variances) is one more mat-vec family. Nothing is
ever materialised.

OptimalInterpolation is the canonical baseline. Every more
sophisticated method must agree with it in the linear-Gaussian limit
(Decision D14 invariant). tests/test_linear_gaussian_agreement.py enforces this for ThreeDVar, StrongFourDVar, WeakFourDVar and IncrementalFourDVar. The block below checks the first two against the BLUE, with M_t the identity and a single time for StrongFourDVar. It prints True twice. Both use a direct cov_solver and 500 minimiser steps, because the smooth prior makes B^{-1} ill-conditioned and BFGS needs about 260 steps here.

import equinox as eqx

# Shapes: S = 1 sample; T = 1 time; N = 20 grid cells; M = 5 along-track samples


# user
class StaticForward(eqx.Module):
    """Trivial dynamics, Mₜ(x) = x: a one-time window is the 3D problem."""

    dt: float = 1.0

    def step(self, state: Float[Array, " n"], dt: float) -> Float[Array, " n"]:
        return state


# today (vardax)
# J(x) = ½ ‖x − x_b‖²_{B⁻¹} + ½ ‖y − H x‖²_{R⁻¹}, minimised iteratively
three_dvar = vdx.ThreeDVar(
    obs_op=model.obs_op,
    prior_mean=climatology_ssh,
    prior_cov_op=prior_cov,
    obs_cov_op=obs_cov,
    cov_solver=lx.AutoLinearSolver(well_posed=True),
    max_steps=500,
)
# StrongFourDVar steps (N,) states, so B, H and R act on one time
cell_structure = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((20,), jnp.float32)
# today (lineax)
# B on (N,) states
cell_cov = lx.FunctionLinearOperator(  # (N, N) PSD op
    kernel_op.mv, cell_structure, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
)
# today (lineax)
along_track_matrix = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(along_track)  # (M, N) op
# today (vardax)
# H x on (N,) states
cell_obs = vdx.LinearObs(operator=along_track_matrix)
# σ_o², one per sample
cell_obs_var = jnp.full(5, obs_std**2)  # (M,)
# today (lineax)
# R = σ_o² I on (M,) observations
cell_obs_cov = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(cell_obs_var)  # (M, M) op
# today (vardax)
# J(x₀) = ½ ‖x₀ − x_b‖²_{B⁻¹} + ½ ‖y − H x₀‖²_{R⁻¹}, with M₀ = I
strong_4dvar = vdx.StrongFourDVar(
    forward=StaticForward(),
    obs_op=cell_obs,
    prior_mean=climatology_ssh[0],
    prior_cov_op=cell_cov,
    obs_cov_op=cell_obs_cov,
    cov_solver=lx.AutoLinearSolver(well_posed=True),
    max_steps=500,
)
# x* = argminₓ J(x), by 3DVar
iterative_3d = three_dvar(batch)  # → (S, T, N)
# x₀* = argmin J(x₀), by strong 4DVar
iterative_4d = strong_4dvar(batch)  # → (S, N)

print(bool(jnp.allclose(x_star, iterative_3d, atol=1e-3)))
print(bool(jnp.allclose(x_star[:, 0], iterative_4d, atol=1e-3)))

Program 4.3:Checks that ThreeDVar minimising 

(5.1) and StrongFourDVar minimising 

(6.1) both reach the BLUE 

(4.4).

If a new method disagrees with OptimalInterpolation in this limit,
something is wrong. The agreement is the definition of correctness.

The Kalman filter analysis step is OI applied at each cycle,\begin{aligned} \text{forecast: } & x^f_t = M_t x^a_{t-1}, \text{ and } P^f_t = M_t P^a_{t-1} M_t^\top + Q \\ \text{analysis: } & K_t = P^f_t H^\top (H P^f_t H^\top + R)^{-1} \\ & x^a_t = x^f_t + K_t (y_t - H x^f_t) \\ & P^a_t = (I - K_t H) P^f_t \end{aligned}

where x^f_t and P^f_t are the forecast mean and covariance, x^a_t and P^a_t the analysis mean and covariance, M_t the linear dynamics and Q the model-error covariance. The analysis lines are 

(4.4) and the first form of 

(4.5).

The analysis step is exactly OptimalInterpolation(prior_mean=x^f_t, prior_cov_op=P^f_t, obs_cov_op=R, obs_op=H).

For a linear-Gaussian state-space model, KalmanSmoother runs the whole recursion exactly: the filter above, then the Rauch–Tung–Striebel smoother backwards, so each x_t is conditioned on every observation in the window. Its transitions act over the actual gaps between observation times, so irregular times need no regridding, and KalmanSmoother.from_sde builds them from a gaussx SDE kernel. The block below smooths an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process observed at four irregular times, the third missing, and prints the smoothed means.

import gaussx as gx
import jax.numpy as jnp
import vardax as vdx

# Shapes: T = 4 times; D_x = D_y = 1

times = jnp.array([0.0, 0.5, 2.0, 2.2])  # (T,)
# today (gaussx)
# OU process: σ² = 1, ℓ = 1
sde = gx.MaternSDE(variance=jnp.asarray(1.0), lengthscale=jnp.asarray(1.0), order=0)
# today (vardax)
# Fₖ = e^{−Δtₖ/ℓ}, Σ_η,ₖ = σ² (1 − e^{−2Δtₖ/ℓ}) on the gaps Δtₖ = tₖ − tₖ₋₁
smoother = vdx.KalmanSmoother.from_sde(
    sde, times, obs_op=jnp.ones((1, 1)), obs_cov=0.1 * jnp.ones((1, 1))
)
obs = jnp.array([[[1.0], [0.8], [jnp.nan], [-0.2]]])  # (S, T, D_y)
mask = jnp.array([[[1.0], [1.0], [0.0], [1.0]]])  # (S, T, D_y)
# today (vardax)
# μₖ|T, k = 1 … T
smoothed = smoother(vdx.Batch1D(input=obs, mask=mask))  # (S, T, D_y) → (S, T, D_x)
print(" ".join(f"{mean:.2f}" for mean in smoothed[0, :, 0]))

Smooths an OU process at irregular times with one missing observation.

It prints 0.93 0.76 -0.08 -0.17: the missing third time is filled from its neighbours, pulled towards the close fourth observation.

The forecast step of an ensemble or nonlinear filter lives in filterax, which composes with OptimalInterpolation for the analysis in the same way.

When OI is the right answer

records.content:
Use OptimalInterpolation when all of:

H is linear (or the linearisation around x_b is good enough that
the residual nonlinearity is dominated by observation noise)

B and R are Gaussian

The posterior is unimodal (no symmetry-breaking, no bistable
regimes)

A single timestep (no dynamics) or the dynamics are linear

If any fails:

Nonlinear H → ThreeDVar (chapter 5)

Dynamics → StrongFourDVar / IncrementalFourDVar (chapters 6, 8)

Non-Gaussian likelihood → AmortizedPosterior with score head (chapter 10)

Multimodal posterior → ensemble methods via filterax

OptimalInterpolation does not check that obs_op is linear: it linearises a nonlinear operator at x_b and returns a single extended-Kalman update, so a nonlinear H belongs in ThreeDVar.

Chapter 2: the observation model (the linear H assumption)

Chapter 5: ThreeDVar (the nonlinear extension)

Chapter 13: posterior covariance (the closed-form P^* is the simplest case)

Design doc: 

design/decisions.md#d16

Lorenc, A. (1981). A global three-dimensional multivariate
statistical interpolation scheme. MWR 109(4).

Daley, R. (1991). Atmospheric Data Analysis. CUP. Ch. 4.

Rasmussen, C. E., & Williams, C. K. I. (2006). Gaussian Processes
for Machine Learning. Ch. 2.7.

When the observation operator H is nonlinear, the closed-form OI analysis 

(4.4) of chapter 4 no longer applies, because the posterior is no longer Gaussian. 3DVar gives up the closed form, keeps the Gaussian prior, and computes the MAP estimate 

(1.2) iteratively.

For a Gaussian prior and likelihood the MAP estimate minimisesJ(x) = \frac{1}{2} \|x - x_b\|^2_{B^{-1}} + \frac{1}{2} \|y - H(x)\|^2_{R^{-1}}

where x_b is the background state, B the background-error covariance, y the observations, H the observation operator 

(2.1) and R the observation-error covariance. Its gradient is\nabla J(x) = B^{-1} (x - x_b) - H'(x)^\top R^{-1} (y - H(x))

where H'(x) is the Jacobian of H at x. The Gauss-Newton approximation of the Hessian isJ''(x) \approx B^{-1} + H'(x)^\top R^{-1} H'(x)

which drops the second-derivative term H''(x)^\top R^{-1} (y - H(x)). That term is small near the MAP when the residual y - H(x) is small, and without it the Hessian is positive-definite, so CG can solve with it.

“3D” refers to the three spatial dimensions of the state; T = 0 in the 4D notation of chapter 1, so there are no dynamics, only one observation set and one inversion.

This is the right regime for:

Snapshot inversions (single satellite overpass, single sounding)

Static fields (long-term mean, climatology)

Multi-instrument fusion at a single time

Methane source attribution from a single overpass (chapter 17)

The example below has a nonlinear operator H(x) = \exp(x), applied cell by cell, on a grid of N = 8 cells at a single time.
The background is x_b = 0 with B = I, the truth is a draw around it, and the observations are y = \exp(x_\text{true}) + \varepsilon with R = \sigma^2 I and \sigma = 0.1.
ThreeDVar takes a batch of S samples, each of shape (T, N).

import einx
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import lineax as lx
import optimistix as optx
import vardax as vdx

# Shapes: S = 1 sample; T = 1 time; N = 8 grid cells

key = jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
key_truth, key_noise = jax.random.split(key)
state_structure = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((1, 8), jnp.float32)

# today (lineax)
# B = I
prior_cov = lx.IdentityLinearOperator(state_structure)  # (T N, T N) op
# today (lineax)
# R = σ² I, σ = 0.1; tagged PSD so the default CG solve accepts it
obs_cov = lx.TaggedLinearOperator(  # (T N, T N) op
    jnp.float32(0.01) * prior_cov, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
)
# x_b = 0
background = jnp.zeros((1, 8))  # (T, N)
# 0.3 δ, δ ~ 𝒩(0, I)
perturbation = 0.3 * jax.random.normal(key_truth, (1, 8))  # (T, N)
# x_true = x_b + 0.3 δ
truth = background + perturbation  # (T, N)
# σ ε, ε ~ 𝒩(0, I)
noise = 0.1 * jax.random.normal(key_noise, (1, 8))  # (T, N)
# exp(x_true)
clean_obs = jnp.exp(truth)  # (T, N)
# y = exp(x_true) + σ ε
obs = clean_obs + noise  # (T, N)

# today (vardax)
# H(x) = exp(x), elementwise
obs_op = vdx.CallableObs(fn=jnp.exp)
# today (vardax)
# J(x) = ½ ‖x − x_b‖²_{B⁻¹} + ½ ‖y − H(x)‖²_{R⁻¹}
model = vdx.ThreeDVar(
    obs_op=obs_op,
    prior_mean=background,
    prior_cov_op=prior_cov,
    obs_cov_op=obs_cov,
    minimiser=optx.BFGS(rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-6),
)
# today (vardax)
batch = vdx.Batch1D(
    input=einx.id("t n -> 1 t n", obs),  # (T, N) → (S, T, N)
    mask=jnp.ones((1, 1, 8)),
)
# x* = argminₓ J(x)
analysis, result = model.analyse(batch)  # → (S, T, N)

# ‖x_b − x_true‖
background_error = jnp.linalg.norm(background - truth)  # → ()
# ‖x* − x_true‖
analysis_error = jnp.linalg.norm(analysis[0] - truth)  # → ()
print(f"background error {background_error:.2f}, analysis error {analysis_error:.2f}")
print(f"converged {bool(result.converged[0])} in {int(result.num_steps[0])} steps")

Program 5.1:Minimises the 3DVar cost 

(5.1) for the nonlinear operator H(x) = exp(x) with ThreeDVar.

It prints background error 0.76, analysis error 0.40 and converged True in 63 steps.

The minimiser is any optimistix.AbstractMinimiser, or a vardax Minimiser such as OptaxMinimiser; the choice depends on the cost function’s geometry:

Minimiser

When

optx.BFGS(...)

General-purpose; no special structure required (the default)

optx.NonlinearCG(...)

Memory-constrained; many parameters

optx.NelderMead(...)

Derivative-free; the cost has kinks

optx.GaussNewton and optx.LevenbergMarquardt are least-squares solvers, not minimisers, so ThreeDVar rejects them; the Gauss-Newton fast path is IncrementalFourDVar (chapter 8).

The minimiser_adjoint controls how gradients flow through the minimiser if the model is itself differentiated through (e.g., for training hyperparameters of B). ImplicitAdjoint is the default; it uses the implicit function theorem at the optimum 

(12.2), which gives exact gradients with O(1) memory. The 4DVar models take the same minimiser= and minimiser_adjoint= slots, and chapter 6 adds a first-order minimiser for large controls.

Written out, 

(5.1) is two whitened quadratic forms, one per term, each applied with a CG solve rather than an inverse.
ThreeDVar builds the same cost, with the residual masked where observations are missing (the mask here is all ones), and hands it to optimistix.minimise.

from jaxtyping import Array, Float

# Shapes: T = 1 time; N = 8 grid cells

# today (lineax)
cov_solver = lx.CG(atol=1e-6, rtol=1e-6)


# user
def threedvar_cost(
    state: Float[Array, "t n"], obs: Float[Array, "t n"]
) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    # δx = x − x_b
    increment = state - background  # (T, N)
    # today (lineax)
    # B⁻¹ δx
    prior_solve = lx.linear_solve(prior_cov, increment, solver=cov_solver)
    # ½ δxᵀ B⁻¹ δx
    background_term = 0.5 * einx.dot("t n, t n ->", increment, prior_solve.value)
    # today (vardax)
    # H(x)
    predicted = obs_op(state)  # (T, N)
    # d = y − H(x)
    innovation = obs - predicted  # (T, N)
    # today (lineax)
    # R⁻¹ d
    obs_solve = lx.linear_solve(obs_cov, innovation, solver=cov_solver)
    # ½ dᵀ R⁻¹ d
    obs_term = 0.5 * einx.dot("t n, t n ->", innovation, obs_solve.value)
    # J(x) = ½ δxᵀ B⁻¹ δx + ½ dᵀ R⁻¹ d
    return background_term + obs_term  # → ()


# today (optimistix)
# x* = argminₓ J(x), started at x_b
solution = optx.minimise(
    threedvar_cost,
    optx.BFGS(rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-6),
    background,
    args=obs,
    adjoint=optx.ImplicitAdjoint(),
    max_steps=200,
)
# the hand-written cost reaches the same minimum as ThreeDVar
print(bool(jnp.allclose(solution.value, analysis[0], atol=1e-3)))

Program 5.2:Writes out the 3DVar cost 

(5.1) by hand and minimises it with optimistix.

Convergence is typically tens of iterations for well-conditioned
problems. The optimistix machinery handles step size, line search, and
termination criteria internally.

When H is linear, the minimum of 

(5.1) is the BLUE 

(4.4), so ThreeDVar must agree with OptimalInterpolation (the Decision D14 invariant, see 

chapter 4). The block below checks it with H = I and the same background and covariances.

# Shapes: S = 1 sample; T = 1 time; N = 8 grid cells

# today (vardax)
# J(x) = ½ ‖x − x_b‖²_{B⁻¹} + ½ ‖y − x‖²_{R⁻¹}, with H = I
linear_three = vdx.ThreeDVar(
    obs_op=vdx.MaskedIdentity(),
    prior_mean=background,
    prior_cov_op=prior_cov,
    obs_cov_op=obs_cov,
)
# today (vardax)
optimal_interpolation = vdx.OptimalInterpolation(
    obs_op=vdx.MaskedIdentity(),
    prior_mean=background,
    prior_cov_op=prior_cov,
    obs_cov_op=obs_cov,
)
# x* = x_b + B Hᵀ (H B Hᵀ + R)⁻¹ (y − H x_b)
closed_form = optimal_interpolation(batch)  # → (S, T, N)
# x* = argminₓ J(x)
iterative = linear_three(batch)  # → (S, T, N)
print(bool(jnp.allclose(closed_form, iterative, atol=1e-3)))

Program 5.3:Checks that ThreeDVar with H = I reaches the BLUE 

(4.4) of OptimalInterpolation.

Near the MAP the Laplace approximation of chapter 13 gives p(x \mid y) \approx \mathcal{N}(x; x^*, P^*), with P^* the Laplace covariance 

(13.1), the inverse of the Gauss-Newton Hessian 

(5.3) at x^*. ThreeDVar.posterior runs the analysis and applies LaplaceCovariance with the model’s B and R; the covariance stays a lazy operator:

# Shapes: S = 1 sample; T = 1 time; N = 8 grid cells

# today (vardax)
# P* = (B⁻¹ + H′(x*)ᵀ R⁻¹ H′(x*))⁻¹
posterior = model.posterior(batch)
# 1, a probe vector
probe = jnp.ones((1, 8))  # (T, N)
# today (vardax)
# P* 1, one matrix-free product
spread = posterior.cov.mv(probe)  # (T, N) → (T, N)

print(posterior.mean.shape, spread.shape)

Program 5.4:Builds the Laplace posterior covariance 

(13.1) of the 3DVar analysis from the Gauss-Newton Hessian 

(5.3).

For strongly nonlinear observation operators the Laplace approximation underestimates uncertainty; EnsembleCovariance (via filterax) or AmortizedPosterior with a flow head calibrate better (chapters 10 and 13).

Use ThreeDVar when H is nonlinear (averaging kernel, RTM, custom retrieval), there is a single time (the regimes listed above), B and R are Gaussian, and a Gaussian around the MAP describes the posterior. If any of these fail:

Linear H: OptimalInterpolation (chapter 4) gives the same answer with an exact posterior.

Dynamics: StrongFourDVar (chapter 6).

Multimodal posterior: the ensemble or amortized methods of the posterior section above.

When the minimiser fails to converge

records.content:
If the minimiser fails (the cost stops decreasing, or the line search rejects every step), the likely causes are:

The cost is far from quadratic: switch from NonlinearCG to BFGS, or relinearise with IncrementalFourDVar (chapter 8) for a 4DVar window.

The prior is too tight (small variance) but biased: widen B or check x_b against innovation statistics.

The observation operator has discontinuities or near-discontinuities (saturated retrievals, mask edges): smooth them in preprocessing or switch to the derivative-free optimistix.NelderMead.

A linear solve inside the cost returns NaN (“A linear solver returned non-finite output”). The cost applies B^{-1} and R^{-1} with lx.CG(atol=1e-6, rtol=1e-6) by default, which breaks down on an ill-conditioned or tiny covariance (an R of 

10-14, say). Pass cov_solver=lx.AutoLinearSolver(well_posed=True) (or lx.Cholesky()) when the operators can be materialised, or rescale the problem so the covariances are O(1). The 4DVar models take the same cov_solver=.

vardax does not retry or fall back automatically, because a failed minimisation is information to diagnose rather than hide. model.analyse(batch) returns the analysis together with a MinimiseResult per sample: the cost and gradient norm at the minimum, the number of steps taken, and converged, the minimiser’s own verdict (optimistix’s result == successful). Read converged rather than comparing num_steps with max_steps: a line search that gives up stops early without converging, and a tolerance can be met on the last allowed step.

Chapter 4: OptimalInterpolation (linear-H closed form)

Chapter 6: StrongFourDVar (add dynamics)

Chapter 8: IncrementalFourDVar (specialised GN+CG inner loop)

Chapter 13: posterior covariance (Laplace and beyond)

Chapter 23: reduced 3DVar, the control in a basis (

(23.4))

Lorenc, A. C. (1986). Analysis methods for numerical weather
prediction. QJRMS 112(474).

Talagrand, O. (1997). Assimilation of observations, an
introduction. JMSJ 75(1B).

Bannister, R. N. (2008). A review of forecast error covariance
statistics in atmospheric variational data assimilation. QJRMS
134(637).

When observations are spread across an assimilation window and the state evolves through known dynamics, 3DVar is no longer enough, because we need to relate observations at later times to the initial state through the forward model. Strong-constraint 4DVar treats the dynamics as exact and makes the initial state x_0 the control variable.

Given observations y_t at times t = 0, 1, \ldots, T, dynamics M_t propagating x_0 to time t, and an observation operator H_t with error covariance R_t at each time, the cost is the 3DVar cost 

(5.1) summed over the window,J(x_0) = \frac{1}{2} \|x_0 - x_b\|^2_{B^{-1}} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{t=0}^{T} \|y_t - H_t(M_t(x_0))\|^2_{R_t^{-1}}

Strong-constraint means the model is treated as exact: any x_0 determines the trajectory 

(1.3) exactly, and model error is not admitted (WeakFourDVar in chapter 7 admits it). The gradient combines the background term with the adjoint of every forward step,\nabla J(x_0) = B^{-1}(x_0 - x_b) + \sum_{t=0}^{T} (M'_t)^\top H'_t{}^\top R_t^{-1} (H_t(M_t(x_0)) - y_t)

where M'_t is the tangent-linear model of M_t at x_0 and H'_t the Jacobian of H_t at M_t(x_0). In hand-coded operational 4DVar, (M'_t)^\top is the adjoint model, historically a major engineering effort (Talagrand and Courtier 1987, Errico 1997). With diffrax, it is a constructor argument.

The example below is Lorenz-96 

(15.2) on N = 40 sites with forcing F = 8, one RK4 step of \Delta t = 0.05 per call, over a window of T = 11 times (10 steps).
The truth x_\text{true} is a state on the attractor; the background is x_b = x_\text{true} + L \xi with B = L L^\top a Gaussian correlation of length scale \ell = 2 sites (plus a 

10-3 jitter), and every second site is observed at every time, y_t = M_t(x_\text{true}) + \varepsilon_t, with R = I.
H_t is the identity on the observed sites, so the mask m_t does the selection.

import dataclasses

import einx
import equinox as eqx
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import lineax as lx
import optimistix as optx
import vardax as vdx
from jaxtyping import Array, Float

# Shapes: S = 1 window; T = 11 times; N = 40 sites

key_spinup, key_background, key_noise, key_field = jax.random.split(
    jax.random.PRNGKey(0), 4
)


# user
class Lorenz96(eqx.Module):
    """Lorenz-96 with forcing F = 8, one RK4 step of length dt per call."""

    dt: float = 0.05

    def tendency(self, state: Float[Array, " n"]) -> Float[Array, " n"]:
        # xₖ₊₁
        east = jnp.roll(state, -1)
        # xₖ₋₂
        far_west = jnp.roll(state, 2)
        # xₖ₋₁
        west = jnp.roll(state, 1)
        # (xₖ₊₁ − xₖ₋₂) xₖ₋₁
        advection = (east - far_west) * west
        # dxₖ/dt = (xₖ₊₁ − xₖ₋₂) xₖ₋₁ − xₖ + F
        return advection - state + 8.0

    def step(self, state: Float[Array, " n"], dt: float) -> Float[Array, " n"]:
        # k₁ = f(x)
        k1 = self.tendency(state)
        # k₂ = f(x + Δt/2 k₁)
        k2 = self.tendency(state + 0.5 * dt * k1)
        # k₃ = f(x + Δt/2 k₂)
        k3 = self.tendency(state + 0.5 * dt * k2)
        # k₄ = f(x + Δt k₃)
        k4 = self.tendency(state + dt * k3)
        # x ← x + Δt/6 (k₁ + 2k₂ + 2k₃ + k₄)
        return state + dt / 6 * (k1 + 2 * k2 + 2 * k3 + k4)


forward = Lorenz96()


# user
def rollout(state: Float[Array, " n"], n_steps: int) -> Float[Array, "t n"]:
    """Return the trajectory x₀, M(x₀), …, Mⁿ(x₀)."""

    def advance(
        carry: Float[Array, " n"], _: None
    ) -> tuple[Float[Array, " n"], Float[Array, " n"]]:
        # xₜ₊₁ = M(xₜ)
        next_state = forward.step(carry, forward.dt)
        return next_state, next_state

    _, later_states = jax.lax.scan(advance, state, length=n_steps)
    # [x₀; x₁ … xₙ]
    return einx.id("n, t n -> (1 + t) n", state, later_states)


site = jnp.arange(40.0)  # (N,)
# i − j
signed_offset = einx.subtract("i, j -> i j", site, site)  # (N, N)
# |i − j|
offset = jnp.abs(signed_offset)  # (N, N)
# dᵢⱼ = min(|i − j|, N − |i − j|), the distance round the ring
distance = jnp.minimum(offset, 40.0 - offset)  # (N, N)
# exp(−dᵢⱼ² / 2ℓ²), ℓ = 2 sites
correlation = jnp.exp(-0.5 * (distance / 2.0) ** 2)  # (N, N)
# 10⁻³ δᵢⱼ
jitter = 1e-3 * jnp.eye(40)  # (N, N)
# Bᵢⱼ = exp(−dᵢⱼ² / 2ℓ²) + 10⁻³ δᵢⱼ
background_corr = correlation + jitter  # (N, N)
# B
prior_cov = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(  # (N, N) PSD op
    background_corr, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
)
# R = I
obs_structure = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((40,), jnp.float32)
obs_cov = lx.IdentityLinearOperator(obs_structure)  # (N, N) op

# δ ~ 𝒩(0, I)
spinup_noise = jax.random.normal(key_spinup, (40,))  # (N,)
# F + δ
spinup_start = 8.0 + spinup_noise  # (N,)
# x_true = M²⁰⁰(F + δ): a state on the attractor
spinup = rollout(spinup_start, 200)  # (N,) → (201, N)
truth_start = spinup[-1]  # (N,)
# B = L Lᵀ
background_chol = jnp.linalg.cholesky(background_corr)  # (N, N)
# ξ ~ 𝒩(0, I)
background_noise = jax.random.normal(key_background, (40,))  # (N,)
# L ξ
background_error = einx.dot(  # (N,)
    "i j, j -> i", background_chol, background_noise
)
# x_b = x_true + L ξ
background = truth_start + background_error  # (N,)
# xₜ = Mₜ(x_true), t = 0 … 10
truth_trajectory = rollout(truth_start, 10)  # (N,) → (T, N)
# εₜ ~ 𝒩(0, I)
obs_noise = jax.random.normal(key_noise, (11, 40))  # (T, N)
# yₜ = Mₜ(x_true) + εₜ
obs = truth_trajectory + obs_noise  # (T, N)
# mₜ = 1 on every second site
mask = jnp.zeros((11, 40)).at[:, ::2].set(1.0)  # (T, N)

# today (vardax)
# J(x₀) = ½ ‖x₀ − x_b‖²_{B⁻¹} + ½ Σₜ ‖mₜ ⊙ (yₜ − Mₜ(x₀))‖²_{R⁻¹}
model = vdx.StrongFourDVar(
    forward=forward,
    obs_op=vdx.MaskedIdentity(),
    prior_mean=background,
    prior_cov_op=prior_cov,
    obs_cov_op=obs_cov,
    minimiser=optx.NonlinearCG(rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-5),
    minimiser_adjoint=optx.ImplicitAdjoint(),
    # recompute each step in reverse mode instead of storing it
    checkpoint=True,
    # this B is too ill-conditioned for the default CG solve
    cov_solver=lx.Cholesky(),
)
obs_window = einx.id("t n -> 1 t n", obs)  # (T, N) → (S, T, N)
mask_window = einx.id("t n -> 1 t n", mask)  # (T, N) → (S, T, N)
# today (vardax)
batch = vdx.Batch1D(input=obs_window, mask=mask_window)
# today (vardax)
# x₀* = argmin J(x₀)
analysis = model(batch)  # → (S, N)


# user
def rmse(state: Float[Array, " n"]) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    """Root-mean-square error of a state against x_true."""
    # (x − x_true)²
    squared_error = (state - truth_start) ** 2  # (N,)
    # mean (x − x_true)²
    mean_squared_error = einx.mean("n ->", squared_error)  # → ()
    # √(mean (x − x_true)²)
    return jnp.sqrt(mean_squared_error)  # → ()


print(f"RMSE of x_b {rmse(background):.2f}, of x₀* {rmse(analysis[0]):.2f}")

Program 6.1:Builds the Lorenz-96 twin experiment and minimises the strong-constraint cost 

(6.1) with NonlinearCG.

It prints RMSE of x_b 1.44, of x₀* 0.63.
With the default lx.CG covariance solver this B (condition number about 5 \times 10^3) makes the B^{-1} solve return non-finite values, so the block passes cov_solver=lx.Cholesky().

Three slots control the gradient:

checkpoint rematerialises the rollout in reverse mode (True, or a block length k), for any per-step forward; the gradient is the same and the memory smaller (chapter 3).

forward_adjoint is a diffrax.AbstractAdjoint for a forward that integrates with diffrax and implements with_adjoint(adjoint) (

SupportsForwardAdjoint), for example dfx.BacksolveAdjoint() for constant memory over long windows. Any other forward raises ValueError.

minimiser_adjoint controls how gradients flow back through the outer minimiser, as for ThreeDVar (chapter 5).

minimiser= takes an optimistix.AbstractMinimiser (the default is optx.BFGS(rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-6); chapter 5 lists the choices) or any 

Minimiser: a callable minimiser(cost_fn, x0, batch) -> x_star over a pytree control. BFGS keeps a dense inverse-Hessian estimate, which is not viable when the control is 

105 network weights. OptaxMinimiser runs a first-order optax optimiser instead, in a jax.lax.while_loop, and stops at max_steps, at a gradient norm below gtol, at a step below atol + rtol·‖x‖, or after patience steps whose cost is worse than the best by more than round-off. (There is no relative cost-change test: next to a large irreducible misfit the cost change rounds to zero in float32 long before x converges.) An optional polish optimiser (e.g. optax.lbfgs()), with its own tight tolerances, finishes from there.

import optax

# today (vardax)
minimiser = vdx.OptaxMinimiser(
    optimizer=optax.adam(1e-2),
    max_steps=2000,
    gtol=1e-4,
    patience=200,
    polish=optax.lbfgs(),
    polish_steps=200,
)
optax_model = dataclasses.replace(model, minimiser=minimiser)
# today (vardax)
# x₀* = argmin J(x₀), by Adam then L-BFGS
optax_analysis = optax_model(batch)  # → (S, N)
print(f"RMSE of x₀* {rmse(optax_analysis[0]):.2f}")

(6.1) of 

Program 6.1 again with Adam, then L-BFGS.

It prints RMSE of x₀* 0.26; the NonlinearCG run above stops at its 200-step cap before it converges.

minimiser_adjoint still applies. Its default, ImplicitAdjoint, is
exact only at a stationary point, \nabla J(x^\star) = 0, which a
first-order optimiser stopped early does not guarantee: OptaxMinimiser
reports \lVert \nabla J(x^\star) \rVert_2 in MinimiseResult.grad_norm;
check it before trusting gradients through the analysis. result.cost
is differentiable (envelope theorem). OptimistixMinimiser() is the default made explicit
and returns exactly what the default model returns.

parameterization= takes any 

StateParameterization: the control becomes a pytree \theta, the initial state x_0 = \psi(\theta), and its penalty replaces the background term of 

(6.1),J(\theta) = \mathrm{pen}(\theta) + \frac{1}{2} \sum_t \lVert y_t - H_t(M_t(\psi(\theta)))\rVert^2_{R_t^{-1}}

where \psi maps the control to the initial state and \mathrm{pen} is the penalty on the control.

LinearParameterization(basis, x_b) is the reduced-basis case
(\psi(X) = x_b + \Phi X, \mathrm{pen}(X) = \frac{1}{2} X^\top Q^{-1} X,
identical to ReducedBasisFourDVar(basis=...)).
NeuralFieldParameterization(field, coords, weight_decay) makes x_0 a
coordinate network evaluated on the grid, with
\mathrm{pen}(\theta) = \frac{\alpha}{2}\lVert\theta\rVert^2 and no B
(the network’s spectral bias is the prior); its weights are a control
for OptaxMinimiser, not BFGS. Frozen arrays inside the field (random
Fourier frequencies read through stop_gradient) must be excluded from
the control with filter_spec=, or the weight decay shrinks them.

The SIREN below has no frozen arrays, so the default filter_spec is right.

# sin λₙ

# sₙ = (cos λₙ, sin λₙ), the sites on the unit circle

# today (vardax)

# J(θ) = pen(θ) + ½ Σₜ ‖mₜ ⊙ (yₜ − Mₜ(ψ(θ)))‖²_{R⁻¹}

    model, parameterization=field_param, minimiser=field_minimiser

# today (vardax)
