ReducedBasisFourDVar(basis=...) minimises this cost with the control moved into a basis, x_0 = x_b + \Phi u with P \ll N coefficients; it is the reduced strong-constraint rung of chapter 

23, which owns its cost 

(23.5), its gradient and the Lorenz-96 comparison against this chapter’s full control.

The gradient 

(6.2) reads “integrate the trajectory forward, then propagate the observation residuals backward through the adjoint of the dynamics.” In equations, this is the backward sweep\lambda_T = H'_T{}^\top R_T^{-1} (H_T(x_T) - y_T)\lambda_{t-1} = (M'_{t \leftarrow t-1})^\top \lambda_t + H'_{t-1}{}^\top R_{t-1}^{-1} (H_{t-1}(x_{t-1}) - y_{t-1})\nabla_{x_0} J = B^{-1}(x_0 - x_b) + \lambda_0

where \lambda_t is the adjoint state at time t and M'_{t \leftarrow t-1} is the tangent-linear model of the single step from t - 1 to t, so that M'_t in 

(6.2) is the product of these one-step tangents. This is exactly what diffrax.RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint or
BacksolveAdjoint compute under the hood. Vardax just composes them
into the cost-gradient call.

Written out, the cost 

(6.1) rolls the trajectory forward, sums the whitened misfit over the window and adds the background term, and optimistix.minimise differentiates through the rollout by reverse mode, which is the backward sweep 

(6.4) to 

(6.6).
StrongFourDVar builds the same cost (with optional jax.checkpoint blocks and a forward_adjoint), so the hand-written one reaches the same minimum.
The block continues the one above.

# Shapes: T = 11 times; N = 40 sites

cov_solver = lx.Cholesky()


# user
def whiten(residual: Float[Array, " n"]) -> Float[Array, " n"]:
    """Apply R⁻¹ to one time's residual with a lineax solve."""
    # R⁻¹ r
    solution = lx.linear_solve(obs_cov, residual, solver=cov_solver)
    return solution.value  # (N,)


# user
def strong_cost(
    initial_state: Float[Array, " n"],
    window: tuple[Float[Array, "t n"], Float[Array, "t n"]],
) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    """Strong-constraint cost J(x₀) over one masked window."""
    window_obs, window_mask = window
    # xₜ = Mₜ(x₀), t = 0 … T − 1
    trajectory = rollout(initial_state, 10)  # (N,) → (T, N)
    # yₜ − Hₜ(xₜ), Hₜ = I
    innovation = window_obs - trajectory  # (T, N)
    # rₜ = mₜ ⊙ (yₜ − Hₜ(xₜ))
    residual = window_mask * innovation  # (T, N)
    # R⁻¹ rₜ at every time
    weighted_residual = jax.vmap(whiten)(residual)  # (T, N)
    # rₜᵀ R⁻¹ rₜ summed over t
    obs_misfit = einx.dot("t n, t n ->", residual, weighted_residual)  # → ()
    # J_o = ½ Σₜ rₜᵀ R⁻¹ rₜ
    obs_term = 0.5 * obs_misfit  # → ()
    # δx = x₀ − x_b
    increment = initial_state - background  # (N,)
    # B⁻¹ δx
    prior_solve = lx.linear_solve(prior_cov, increment, solver=cov_solver)
    # δxᵀ B⁻¹ δx
    prior_misfit = einx.dot("n, n ->", increment, prior_solve.value)  # → ()
    # J_b = ½ δxᵀ B⁻¹ δx
    background_term = 0.5 * prior_misfit  # → ()
    # J(x₀) = J_b + J_o
    return background_term + obs_term  # → ()


# today (optimistix)
# x₀* = argmin J(x₀), started at x_b
solution = optx.minimise(
    strong_cost,
    optx.NonlinearCG(rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-5),
    background,
    args=(obs, mask),
    adjoint=optx.ImplicitAdjoint(),
    max_steps=200,
    throw=False,
)
print(bool(jnp.allclose(solution.value, analysis[0], atol=1e-3)))

# today (vardax)
# x₀* = argmin J(x₀), with J(x₀*) and ‖∇J(x₀*)‖ as diagnostics
result = minimiser.run(strong_cost, background, (obs, mask))
print(f"J = {result.cost:.1f}, ‖∇J‖ = {result.grad_norm:.1e}")

For T = 100+ assimilation cycles, the forward trajectory dominates
memory. Four strategies:

checkpoint=True (or a block length). Works with any per-step forward, with 3 to 4 times less gradient memory on Lorenz-96 (chapter 3).

dfx.BacksolveAdjoint() (via forward_adjoint=, for a 

SupportsForwardAdjoint forward) solves the adjoint ODE backwards in time, with O(1) memory in the trajectory length. Reverse-time stiffness can require an implicit integrator (dfx.Kvaerno5, dfx.ImplicitEuler).

dfx.RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint(checkpoints=N) (also via forward_adjoint=) stores N checkpoints and recomputes the segments between them, with O(\sqrt{T}) memory.

Shorter windows. Run multiple StrongFourDVar analyses with
shorter windows and cycle them via pipekit_cycle.DACycle. This is
what operational systems do.

For most research-scale problems with T \le 20, the defaults
(plain reverse mode, the forward’s own adjoint) are fine.

The 4DVar cost 

(6.1) is nonconvex when M_t is nonlinear, so multiple local minima exist (and matter, especially for chaotic systems like Lorenz). Strategies:

Multi-start. Minimise from several perturbed first guesses and
keep the lowest cost. vardax has no helper for this yet: the models
start every minimisation from x_b, so a multi-start needs a first
guess separate from the background.

Quasi-static gradient. Use a warm-start from a previous cycle
(the usual operational pattern).

Switch to IncrementalFourDVar (chapter 8): the outer Gauss-Newton iterations relinearise around the current iterate, which is more robust than NonlinearCG on the full nonlinear cost.

Pair the analysis with a PosteriorAdapter; LaplaceCovariance returns the Gauss-Newton covariance 

(13.2) of chapter 13 as a lazy operator. The block continues the one above.
It passes solver=lx.Cholesky() because the default CG solve of B^{-1} reaches its step cap on this B; model.posterior(batch, adapter=laplace) is the same call.

# 1

# P* 1, one matrix-free product

records.content: Use StrongFourDVar for multi-time observations with dynamics when model error is small (within the noise floor of the observations) and you want an optimistix or optax minimiser directly on the full nonlinear cost. For operational 4DVar with structured priors, IncrementalFourDVar solves the same problem faster; chapter 8 says when to switch. If model error matters, use WeakFourDVar (chapter 7).

Strong-constraint 4DVar (chapter 6) treats the forward model as exact. For real systems this is wrong, as models have biases, missing physics and discretisation error. Over long assimilation windows the trajectory drifts away from the observations because the model itself is wrong, even when the analysis is good. Weak-constraint 4DVar admits this model error as an additional control variable.

The state evolves under noisy dynamics,x_t = M_t^\text{free}(x_{t-1}) + \eta_t, \text{ with } \eta_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, Q_t)

where M_t^\text{free} is the single model step from t - 1 to t, \eta_t the model error of that step and Q_t its covariance. The control vector is augmented from x_0 to (x_0, \eta_1, \ldots, \eta_T), and the strong cost 

(6.1) gains a model-error term:J(x_0, \boldsymbol{\eta}) = \underbrace{\frac{1}{2} \|x_0 - x_b\|^2_{B^{-1}}}_{\text{background}} + \underbrace{\frac{1}{2} \sum_t \|y_t - H_t(x_t)\|^2_{R_t^{-1}}}_{\text{observations}} + \underbrace{\frac{1}{2} \sum_t \|\eta_t\|^2_{Q_t^{-1}}}_{\text{model error}}

where the trajectory x_t is recovered from (x_0, \boldsymbol{\eta}) by stepping 

(7.1) forward from x_0.

Two failure modes of strong-constraint 4DVar:

Climatological drift. The free model’s climatology differs from reality. Long windows produce x_T far from y_T regardless of x_0, and the analysis tries to compensate by moving x_0, which damages the early-time fit.

Missing fast physics. The model resolves the slow manifold but
not the fast (cloud microphysics, sub-grid turbulence). Strong 4DVar
attributes fast-physics errors to x_0, which is the wrong place.

Allowing \eta_t to absorb these errors per-step gives a better fit at
every time without distorting x_0.

The example below has N = 8 sites and a window of T = 6 times (5 steps).
The free model decays every site, M^\text{free}(x) = 0.8 x, but the truth also gains a constant 0.5 per step, x_t = 0.8 x_{t-1} + 0.5, which the free model misses.
Every site is observed at every time with R = 0.01 I; the background is x_b = 0 with B = I, and the model-error covariance is Q = 0.04 I.

import einx
import equinox as eqx
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import lineax as lx
import optimistix as optx
import vardax as vdx
from jaxtyping import Array, Float

# Shapes: S = 1 window; T = 6 times; N = 8 sites

key_truth, key_noise = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(0))


# user
class Decay(eqx.Module):
    """The free model M^free(x) = 0.8 x, missing the truth's forcing."""

    dt: float = 1.0

    def step(self, state: Float[Array, " n"], dt: float) -> Float[Array, " n"]:
        # M^free(x) = 0.8 x
        return 0.8 * state


# user
def truth_step(
    state: Float[Array, " n"], _: None
) -> tuple[Float[Array, " n"], Float[Array, " n"]]:
    """One step of the true dynamics, with the forcing the free model misses."""
    # xₜ = 0.8 xₜ₋₁ + 0.5
    next_state = 0.8 * state + 0.5  # (N,)
    return next_state, next_state


psd = lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
state_structure = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((8,), jnp.float32)
# B = I
prior_cov = lx.IdentityLinearOperator(state_structure)  # (N, N) op
# R = 0.01 I, tagged PSD so the default CG solve accepts it
obs_cov = lx.TaggedLinearOperator(0.01 * prior_cov, psd)  # (N, N) PSD op
# Q = 0.04 I
model_err_cov = lx.TaggedLinearOperator(0.04 * prior_cov, psd)  # (N, N) PSD op
# x_b = 0
background = jnp.zeros(8)  # (N,)
# x₀ ~ 𝒩(0, I)
truth_start = jax.random.normal(key_truth, (8,))  # (N,)
# x₁ … x₅ under the true dynamics
_, truth_later = jax.lax.scan(truth_step, truth_start, length=5)  # (T − 1, N)
# [x₀; x₁ … x₅]
truth = einx.id("n, t n -> (1 + t) n", truth_start, truth_later)  # (T, N)
# εₜ ~ 𝒩(0, I)
obs_noise = jax.random.normal(key_noise, (6, 8))  # (T, N)
# yₜ = xₜ + 0.1 εₜ
obs = truth + 0.1 * obs_noise  # (T, N)

# today (vardax)
# J(x₀, η) = ½ ‖x₀ − x_b‖²_{B⁻¹} + ½ Σₜ ‖yₜ − xₜ‖²_{R⁻¹} + ½ Σₜ ‖ηₜ‖²_{Q⁻¹}
model = vdx.WeakFourDVar(
    forward=Decay(),
    obs_op=vdx.MaskedIdentity(),
    prior_mean=background,
    prior_cov_op=prior_cov,
    obs_cov_op=obs_cov,
    model_err_cov_op=model_err_cov,
    minimiser=optx.NonlinearCG(rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-5),
    # chapter 3
    checkpoint=True,
)
obs_window = einx.id("t n -> 1 t n", obs)  # (T, N) → (S, T, N)
# mₜ = 1 everywhere
all_observed = jnp.ones((1, 6, 8))  # (S, T, N)
# today (vardax)
batch = vdx.Batch1D(input=obs_window, mask=all_observed)
# today (vardax)
# (x₀*, η*) = argmin J(x₀, η): the analysis IC and the model-error trajectory
initial_star, model_error_star = model(batch)  # → (S, N), (S, T − 1, N)

# today (vardax)
# J(x₀) = ½ ‖x₀ − x_b‖²_{B⁻¹} + ½ Σₜ ‖yₜ − Mₜ(x₀)‖²_{R⁻¹}, no model-error term
strong = vdx.StrongFourDVar(
    forward=Decay(),
    obs_op=vdx.MaskedIdentity(),
    prior_mean=background,
    prior_cov_op=prior_cov,
    obs_cov_op=obs_cov,
    minimiser=optx.NonlinearCG(rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-5),
)
# today (vardax)
# x₀* = argmin J(x₀)
strong_initial = strong(batch)  # → (S, N)
# x₀* − x₀ for each method
weak_offset = initial_star[0] - truth_start  # (N,)
strong_offset = strong_initial[0] - truth_start  # (N,)
# ‖x₀* − x₀‖
weak_error = jnp.linalg.norm(weak_offset)  # → ()
strong_error = jnp.linalg.norm(strong_offset)  # → ()
# mean of η*, against the missing forcing 0.5
mean_model_error = einx.mean("s t n ->", model_error_star)  # → ()
print(f"x₀ error: strong {strong_error:.2f}, weak {weak_error:.2f}")
print(f"mean η* {mean_model_error:.2f}")

Program 7.1:Minimises the weak-constraint cost 

(7.2) and, for comparison, the strong cost 

(6.1) on a window whose free model misses a constant forcing.

It prints x₀ error: strong 2.81, weak 0.25 and mean η* 0.46: the strong analysis moves x_0 to make up for the missing forcing, while the weak analysis puts it into \eta.

The model error covariance Q is a separate input. Three common
parameterisations:

Diagonal: lineax.DiagonalLinearOperator(variances), white Gaussian model noise. Simple but rarely realistic.

Matérn spatial: kernellib.ImplicitKernelOperator(matern, coords) with a Matérn kernel function, for spatially correlated model error.

Markovian time-correlated: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Q_t with correlation timescale \tau. The error decorrelates over \tau steps, which is physically motivated.

The choice of Q is the single most important tuning choice in weak-constraint 4DVar. Too tight, and the result reverts to strong; too loose, and the observations dominate the analysis to the exclusion of the dynamics.

The control vector dimension grows with T:\dim(\text{control}) = \dim(x_0) + T \cdot \dim(x_t)

For T = 100 and a 2D field with n = 10^4, this is \sim 10^6
control variables instead of 

104. The minimisation is correspondingly
heavier. Two mitigations:

Lower-rank model-error parameterisation. Restrict \eta_t to a
low-dimensional subspace (POD modes, learned latent space). vardax
does not provide this out of the box; users supply a custom
reparameterisation via an eqx.Module.

Shorter sub-windows. Run weak-constraint 4DVar over a short
sub-window where \eta_t dimensionality is manageable, cycle the
result via pipekit_cycle.SmootherCycle. Operational ECMWF uses
this pattern.

For T = 0, \eta is empty and 

(7.2) is the 3DVar cost 

(5.1), whose minimum for linear H is the BLUE 

(4.4); this is the Decision D14 invariant of 

chapter 4. The block continues the one above with the first time only:

# Shapes: S = 1 window; T = 1 time; N = 8 sites

# y₀ and m₀ only
first_obs = batch.input[:, :1]  # (S, T, N)
first_mask = batch.mask[:, :1]  # (S, T, N)
# today (vardax)
first_time = vdx.Batch1D(input=first_obs, mask=first_mask)
# B = I and R = 0.01 I over OI's (T, N) state
field_structure = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((1, 8), jnp.float32)
field_prior_cov = lx.IdentityLinearOperator(field_structure)  # (T N, T N) op
field_obs_diag = jnp.full((1, 8), 0.01)  # (T, N)
field_obs_cov = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(field_obs_diag)  # (T N, T N) op
# today (vardax)
# p(x) = 𝒩(0, B), p(y | x) = 𝒩(x, R)
optimal_interpolation = vdx.OptimalInterpolation(
    obs_op=vdx.MaskedIdentity(),
    prior_mean=jnp.zeros((1, 8)),
    prior_cov_op=field_prior_cov,
    obs_cov_op=field_obs_cov,
)
# today (vardax)
# x_a = x_b + B Hᵀ (H B Hᵀ + R)⁻¹ (y − H x_b)
closed_form = optimal_interpolation(first_time)  # → (S, T, N)
# today (vardax)
# (x₀*, η*) = argmin J(x₀, η); Q is unused when T = 0
weak_initial, weak_model_error = model(first_time)  # → (S, N), (S, 0, N)
print(bool(jnp.allclose(closed_form[:, 0], weak_initial, atol=1e-3)))
print(weak_model_error.shape)

Program 7.2:Checks that the weak-constraint minimum of 

(7.2) with T = 0 equals the BLUE 

(4.4) and that η is empty.

It prints True and (1, 0, 8): \eta is empty when T = 0.

For T > 0 and a very tight Q (precision Q^{-1} \to \infty), \eta_t \to 0 and 

(7.2) reduces to 

(6.1), so WeakFourDVar reduces to StrongFourDVar. This weak-to-strong limit can be tested too.

The posterior is over the augmented control vector (x_0, \boldsymbol{\eta}), and the Laplace approximation 

(13.1) of chapter 13 gives a Gaussian on this space, whose precision gains Q^{-1} on each \eta_t. LaplaceCovariance returns its x_0 block:

# Shapes: N = 8 sites; T = 6 times

# today (vardax)
laplace = vdx.LaplaceCovariance()
# today (vardax)
analysis_step = model.as_analysis_step()
# (x₀*, η*) for the one window
control_star = (initial_star[0], model_error_star[0])  # (N,), (T − 1, N)
# today (vardax)
# P* = [(Λ_GN)⁻¹]ₓ₀ₓ₀, Λ_GN the Gauss-Newton precision over (x₀, η)
posterior = laplace(control_star, analysis_step, batch)
# 1
ones = jnp.ones(8)  # (N,)
# P* 1, one matrix-free product on the state
spread = posterior.cov.mv(ones)  # (N,) → (N,)
print(posterior.mean.shape, spread.shape)

Program 7.3:Builds the x₀ block of the Laplace covariance 

(13.1) over the augmented control (x₀, η) of 

(7.2) and applies it to one vector.

It prints (8,) (8,): the mean is x_0^* and the covariance is the x_0 block of the inverse augmented precision, a lazy operator on the state, not the whole augmented covariance; model.posterior(batch) returns the same.

For the marginal posterior on the state trajectory \{x_t\}_{t=0}^T,
apply the forward at each time and propagate the covariance. This is
implementation-heavy and rarely needed; ensemble approaches via
filterax are usually preferable when full trajectory uncertainty
matters.

records.content:
Use WeakFourDVar for multi-time observations when the model is known to have biases (the two failure modes above), strong-constraint analyses misfit the later times of a long window, and you have a reasonable model-error covariance Q_t (often from comparing the free model to higher-fidelity runs or to reanalyses). If model error is small (within the observation noise), use StrongFourDVar (chapter 6), since the extra control variables are not worth the cost.

If you’d rather replace the parametric prior with a learned one,
FourDVarNet (chapter 9) is the alternative. The learned prior
absorbs the same kind of model error that \eta_t would, without an
explicit augmented control.

Chapter 6: StrongFourDVar (the no-model-error baseline)

Chapter 9: FourDVarNet (learned alternative to weak-constraint)

Chapter 13: posterior covariance (augmented-state case)

Chapter 23: reduced weak-constraint 4DVar, a model error in a basis (

(23.10))

Trémolet, Y. (2006). Accounting for an imperfect model in 4D-Var.
QJRMS 132(621).

Fisher, M., Leutbecher, M., & Kelly, G. A. (2005). On the equivalence
between Kalman smoothing and weak-constraint four-dimensional
variational data assimilation. QJRMS 131(613).

Daescu, D. N., & Todling, R. (2010). Adjoint sensitivity of the
model forecast to data assimilation system error covariance
parameters. QJRMS 136(653).

Operational 4DVar at ECMWF, NCEP, JMA, and UKMO all follow a common
template: Gauss-Newton outer iterations on the full nonlinear cost,
CG (or Lanczos) inner iterations on a linearised quadratic
subproblem, with a control-variable transform that preconditions the
inner solve. IncrementalFourDVar packages this pattern.

It solves the same problem as StrongFourDVar (chapter 6) and gives the same answer, but the specialised inner solver is much faster when the prior is structured (Matérn, Kronecker) and the window is long.

Strong-constraint 4DVar minimises 

(6.1). Write x^{(k)} for the outer iterate, starting from x^{(0)} = x_b. The background x_b stays fixed across outer loops; only x^{(k)} moves. Linearise around x^{(k)}:M_t(x^{(k)} + \delta x) \approx M_t(x^{(k)}) + M'_t \delta xH_t(z + \delta z) \approx H_t(z) + H'_t \delta z

where M'_t = \partial M_t / \partial x|_{x^{(k)}} from
jax.linearize and H'_t is the tangent of H_t at
M_t(x^{(k)}). With the innovation
d_t^{(k)} = y_t - H_t(M_t(x^{(k)})), the linearised (quadratic)
cost of an increment \delta x is\delta J(\delta x) = \frac{1}{2} \|x^{(k)} + \delta x - x_b\|^2_{B^{-1}} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_t \|d_t^{(k)} - H'_t M'_t \delta x\|^2_{R_t^{-1}}

The background term measures the total departure x^{(k)} + \delta x - x_b, not \delta x alone. The Gauss-Newton Hessian is\mathbf{H}_\text{GN} = B^{-1} + \sum_t (H'_t M'_t)^\top R_t^{-1} (H'_t M'_t)

which is the 4DVar form of the 3DVar Hessian 

(5.3). Setting \nabla \delta J = 0 gives the inner system that the CG (or Lanczos) solver solves for \delta x^*:\mathbf{H}_\text{GN} \delta x^* = -B^{-1}\left(x^{(k)} - x_b\right) + \sum_t (H'_t M'_t)^\top R_t^{-1} d_t^{(k)} = -\nabla J\left(x^{(k)}\right)

The right-hand side is the negative gradient 

(6.2) of the full nonlinear cost at the current iterate. On the first outer loop x^{(0)} = x_b, so the background term vanishes and only the innovation term is left. On later loops it does not vanish: dropping it would pull every increment toward x^{(k)} instead of x_b, and the iteration would no longer converge to the 4DVar minimum.

Outer update: x^{(k+1)} = x^{(k)} + \delta x^*. Relinearise.

This pattern converges in a handful of outer iterations (typically 3 to 5) regardless of the strength of the nonlinearity, because each outer step sees a fresh tangent linearisation.

The Hessian \mathbf{H}_\text{GN} inherits the condition number of
B^{-1}: a smooth (long-correlation) B has tiny eigenvalues, which
become huge ones of B^{-1}. In state space every Hessian product also
needs B^{-1}v, which IncrementalFourDVar would have to compute by a
nested CG solve.

The CVT changes variables. Let S be a square root of B, S S^\top = B,
and write the departure from the background asx_0 - x_b = S \chi

The background term becomes \frac{1}{2}\|x_0 - x_b\|^2_{B^{-1}} =
\frac{1}{2}\|\chi\|^2, and the inner system at the outer iterate
\chi^{(k)} becomes\left(I + S^\top G'^\top R^{-1} G' S\right) \delta\chi^* = -\nabla_\chi J\left(\chi^{(k)}\right) = -\chi^{(k)} + S^\top G'^\top R^{-1} d^{(k)}

where G' stacks H'_t M'_t over the window. Its eigenvalues are all
\ge 1, close to 1 in directions the observations barely see, and no
B^{-1} appears anywhere. The outer update is
\chi^{(k+1)} = \chi^{(k)} + \delta\chi^*, and the analysis is
x_0^* = x_b + S\chi^*.

IncrementalConfig(cvt=True) (the default) uses it. S is
prior_sqrt_op= when given (a Cholesky factor, a structured
operator’s own square root, or gaussx.sqrt(B, lanczos_order=k) for a
large unstructured B), else gaussx.sqrt(prior_cov_op): closed form
for diagonal, Kronecker and block-diagonal B, a dense
eigendecomposition otherwise. cvt=False keeps the state-space solve,
with B^{-1} and R^{-1} applied by CG at tolerance
covariance_tol.

How much it helps. A linear problem with 20 states, 4 times, every
third site observed, a Gaussian-kernel B of length scale 3 sites plus
a diagonal jitter that sets its condition number; inner CG iterations to
reach 

10-4 relative error on the exact analysis:

The CVT count does not grow with \kappa(B), and each state-space
iteration also runs a nested CG for B^{-1}v. For a well-conditioned
B the two are comparable.

The example below is a 4 \times 5 grid (N = 20 cells) over a window of T = 4 times, with a nonlinear forward M(x) = x + 0.2 \sin(x) applied cell by cell.
B = B_y \otimes B_x is separable, each factor a Gaussian correlation of length scale 1.5 cells (plus a 

10-1 jitter), and the background is x_b = 0.
Every cell is observed through an averaging kernel 

(2.5) with A = I, h = 0.8 and x_a = 0, and R = 0.04 I.

import einx
import equinox as eqx
import gaussx as gx
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import lineax as lx
import optimistix as optx
import vardax as vdx
from jaxtyping import Array, Float

# Shapes: S = 1 window; T = 4 times; N = Y X = 20 cells; Y = 4 rows; X = 5 columns

key_truth, key_noise = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(0))


# user
class SineDrift(eqx.Module):
    """A toy nonlinear forward, M(x) = x + 0.2 sin(x), cell by cell."""

    dt: float = 1.0

    def step(self, state: Float[Array, " n"], dt: float) -> Float[Array, " n"]:
        # sin(x)
        drift = jnp.sin(state)
        # M(x) = x + 0.2 Δt sin(x)
        return state + 0.2 * dt * drift


# user
def gaussian_corr(n_cells: int) -> lx.MatrixLinearOperator:
    """Gaussian correlation of length scale 1.5 cells, plus a 10⁻¹ jitter."""
    cell = jnp.arange(float(n_cells))  # (n,)
    # dᵢⱼ = i − j
    offset = einx.subtract("i, j -> i j", cell, cell)  # (n, n)
    # exp(−dᵢⱼ² / 2ℓ²), ℓ = 1.5 cells
    correlation = jnp.exp(-0.5 * (offset / 1.5) ** 2)  # (n, n)
    # 10⁻¹ δᵢⱼ
    jitter = 1e-1 * jnp.eye(n_cells)  # (n, n)
    # Cᵢⱼ = exp(−dᵢⱼ² / 2ℓ²) + 10⁻¹ δᵢⱼ
    corr = correlation + jitter  # (n, n)
    return lx.MatrixLinearOperator(corr, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag)


forward = SineDrift()
# B_y
row_corr = gaussian_corr(4)  # (Y, Y) PSD op
# B_x
col_corr = gaussian_corr(5)  # (X, X) PSD op
# today (gaussx)
# B = B_y ⊗ B_x, whose square root gaussx.sqrt computes factor by factor
prior_cov = gx.Kronecker(  # (N, N) PSD op
    row_corr, col_corr, tags=lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
)
# A = I
kernel_matrix = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(jnp.eye(20))  # (N, N) op
# x_a = 0
prior_profile = jnp.zeros(20)  # (N,)
# h = 0.8
pressure_weights = jnp.full(20, 0.8)  # (N,)
# today (vardax)
# H(x) = A (h ⊙ x + (1 − h) ⊙ x_a)
obs_op = vdx.AveragingKernel(
    kernel_matrix=kernel_matrix,
    prior_profile=prior_profile,
    pressure_weights=pressure_weights,
)
# diag(R) = 0.04
obs_diag = jnp.full(20, 0.04)  # (N,)
# R = 0.04 I, tagged PSD for the Cholesky solve below
obs_cov = lx.TaggedLinearOperator(  # (N, N) PSD op
    lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(obs_diag), lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
)
# x_b = 0
background = jnp.zeros(20)  # (N,)
# B as a dense matrix
prior_matrix = prior_cov.as_matrix()  # (N, N)
# B = L Lᵀ
prior_chol = jnp.linalg.cholesky(prior_matrix)  # (N, N)
# ξ ~ 𝒩(0, I)
truth_noise = jax.random.normal(key_truth, (20,))  # (N,)
# x₀ = L ξ
truth_start = einx.dot("i j, j -> i", prior_chol, truth_noise)  # (N,)


# user
def advance(
    state: Float[Array, " n"], _: None
) -> tuple[Float[Array, " n"], Float[Array, " n"]]:
    """One forward step, in the carry-and-output form of jax.lax.scan."""
    # xₜ₊₁ = M(xₜ)
    next_state = forward.step(state, forward.dt)  # (N,)
    return next_state, next_state


# x₁ … x₃
_, truth_later = jax.lax.scan(advance, truth_start, length=3)  # (T − 1, N)
# [x₀; x₁ … x₃]
truth = einx.id("n, t n -> (1 + t) n", truth_start, truth_later)  # (T, N)
# H(xₜ) at every time
truth_observed = jax.vmap(obs_op)(truth)  # (T, N)
# εₜ ~ 𝒩(0, I)
obs_noise = jax.random.normal(key_noise, (4, 20))  # (T, N)
# yₜ = H(xₜ) + 0.2 εₜ
obs = truth_observed + 0.2 * obs_noise  # (T, N)

# today (vardax)
# x⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾ = x⁽ᵏ⁾ + δx*, (I + Sᵀ G′ᵀ R⁻¹ G′ S) δχ* = −∇_χ J
model = vdx.IncrementalFourDVar(
    forward=forward,
    obs_op=obs_op,
    prior_mean=background,
    prior_cov_op=prior_cov,
    obs_cov_op=obs_cov,
    config=vdx.IncrementalConfig(n_outer=3, n_inner=20, cvt=True),
)
obs_window = einx.id("t n -> 1 t n", obs)  # (T, N) → (S, T, N)
# mₜ = 1 everywhere
all_observed = jnp.ones((1, 4, 20))  # (S, T, N)
# today (vardax)
batch = vdx.Batch1D(input=obs_window, mask=all_observed)
# today (vardax)
# x₀* after three Gauss-Newton outer loops
analysis = model(batch)  # → (S, N)

# today (vardax)
# J(x₀) = ½ ‖x₀ − x_b‖²_{B⁻¹} + ½ Σₜ ‖yₜ − H(Mₜ(x₀))‖²_{R⁻¹}, minimised directly
strong = vdx.StrongFourDVar(
    forward=forward,
    obs_op=obs_op,
    prior_mean=background,
    prior_cov_op=prior_cov,
    obs_cov_op=obs_cov,
    minimiser=optx.BFGS(rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-6),
    cov_solver=lx.Cholesky(),
)
# today (vardax)
# x₀* = argmin J(x₀)
strong_analysis = strong(batch)  # → (S, N)
# x₀ⁱⁿᶜ − x₀ˢᵗʳᵒⁿᵍ
gap = analysis - strong_analysis  # (S, N)
# |x₀ⁱⁿᶜ − x₀ˢᵗʳᵒⁿᵍ|
abs_gap = jnp.abs(gap)  # (S, N)
# max |x₀ⁱⁿᶜ − x₀ˢᵗʳᵒⁿᵍ|
largest_gap = einx.max("s n ->", abs_gap)  # → ()
print(f"largest gap to StrongFourDVar {largest_gap:.1e}")

# today (vardax)
# Gauss-Newton posterior at the analysis, with the model's B and R
posterior = model.posterior(batch)

Program 8.1:Solves the control-variable system 

(8.7) in each outer loop of incremental 4DVar and compares the analysis with the direct minimum of 

(6.1).

It prints largest gap to StrongFourDVar 2.0e-03: three outer loops of at most 20 CG steps each land that close to the BFGS minimum of the same cost.

IncrementalConfig:

n_outer: number of Gauss-Newton outer iterations (typically 3).

n_inner: maximum CG iterations per outer iteration (typically 20 to 50); the inner solve is truncated there.

cg_atol, cg_rtol: inner CG convergence tolerances.

cvt: solve over \chi of 

(8.6) (default True).

covariance_tol: tolerance of the CG solves that apply R^{-1} (and B^{-1} when cvt=False).

jac: "fwd" (default) applies H'_t M'_t by jax.linearize, matrix-free. "bwd" forms the window’s Jacobian with jax.jacrev, one VJP per observation, and runs CG on that matrix. Pass it when the forward or observation map defines only a reverse-mode rule, such as a jax.custom_vjp or a diffrax solve under RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint; it suits windows of up to a few thousand observations, and the posterior uses the same mode.

A static control, such as a source field rather than an initial state, is an identity-step forward (step returns its input) with a one-time window: the outer loop is then Gauss-Newton 3D-Var through any obs_op.

Written out with the control-variable transform, each outer loop linearises the observed trajectory G(x) = [H_t(M_t(x))]_t once and hands the inner system 

(8.7) to CG, then maps the control back through 

(8.6).
The block continues the one above and reproduces model(batch).

# Shapes: T = 4 times; N = 20 cells

config = model.config
covariance_solver = lx.CG(atol=config.covariance_tol, rtol=config.covariance_tol)
inner_solver = lx.CG(atol=config.cg_atol, rtol=config.cg_rtol, max_steps=config.n_inner)
state_struct = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((20,), jnp.float32)
# today (gaussx)
# S Sᵀ = B, here S = S_y ⊗ S_x
prior_sqrt = gx.sqrt(prior_cov)  # (N, N) op
# Sᵀ
prior_sqrt_t = prior_sqrt.transpose()  # (N, N) op


# user
def observed_trajectory(state: Float[Array, " n"]) -> Float[Array, "t n"]:
    """The observed trajectory G(x) = [Hₜ(Mₜ(x))]ₜ."""
    # x₁ … x₃
    _, later_states = jax.lax.scan(advance, state, length=3)  # (T − 1, N)
    # [x₀; x₁ … x₃]
    trajectory = einx.id("n, t n -> (1 + t) n", state, later_states)  # (T, N)
    # G(x) = [Hₜ(Mₜ(x))]ₜ
    return jax.vmap(obs_op)(trajectory)  # (T, N)


# user
def whiten_one(residual: Float[Array, " n"]) -> Float[Array, " n"]:
    """Apply R⁻¹ to one time's residual with a lineax solve."""
    # R⁻¹ r
    solution = lx.linear_solve(obs_cov, residual, solver=covariance_solver)
    return solution.value  # (N,)


# user
def whiten(residual: Float[Array, "t n"]) -> Float[Array, "t n"]:
    """Apply R⁻¹ at every time of the window."""
    # R⁻¹ rₜ at every time
    return jax.vmap(whiten_one)(residual)  # (T, N)


# χ⁽⁰⁾ = 0, so x⁽⁰⁾ = x_b
control = jnp.zeros(20)  # (N,)
for _ in range(config.n_outer):
    # S χ⁽ᵏ⁾
    increment = prior_sqrt.mv(control)  # (N,)
    # x⁽ᵏ⁾ = x_b + S χ⁽ᵏ⁾
    state = background + increment  # (N,)
    # G(x⁽ᵏ⁾) and v ↦ G′ v, the tangent of the observed trajectory
    predicted, tangent = jax.linearize(observed_trajectory, state)  # (T, N)
    # w ↦ G′ᵀ w, its adjoint
    adjoint = jax.linear_transpose(tangent, state)
    # dᵏ = y − G(x⁽ᵏ⁾)
    innovation = obs - predicted  # (T, N)
    # R⁻¹ dᵏ
    weighted_innovation = whiten(innovation)  # (T, N)
    # G′ᵀ R⁻¹ dᵏ
    (obs_gradient,) = adjoint(weighted_innovation)  # (T, N) → (N,)
    # Sᵀ G′ᵀ R⁻¹ dᵏ
    control_obs_gradient = prior_sqrt_t.mv(obs_gradient)  # (N,)
    # −∇_χ J(χ⁽ᵏ⁾) = −χ⁽ᵏ⁾ + Sᵀ G′ᵀ R⁻¹ dᵏ
    rhs = -control + control_obs_gradient  # (N,)

    # user
    def hessian_mv(direction: Float[Array, " n"]) -> Float[Array, " n"]:
        """The CVT Hessian product (I + Sᵀ G′ᵀ R⁻¹ G′ S) v."""
        # S v
        state_direction = prior_sqrt.mv(direction)  # (N,)
        # G′ S v
        observed_direction = tangent(state_direction)  # (T, N)
        # R⁻¹ G′ S v
        weighted_direction = whiten(observed_direction)  # (T, N)
        # G′ᵀ R⁻¹ G′ S v
        (back_projected,) = adjoint(weighted_direction)  # (T, N) → (N,)
        # Sᵀ G′ᵀ R⁻¹ G′ S v
        control_back_projected = prior_sqrt_t.mv(back_projected)  # (N,)
        # (I + Sᵀ G′ᵀ R⁻¹ G′ S) v
        return direction + control_back_projected  # (N,)

    # I + Sᵀ G′ᵀ R⁻¹ G′ S, eigenvalues ≥ 1
    inner_hessian = lx.FunctionLinearOperator(  # (N, N) PSD op
        hessian_mv, state_struct, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
    )
    # δχ* from truncated CG
    step = lx.linear_solve(inner_hessian, rhs, solver=inner_solver, throw=False)
    # χ⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾ = χ⁽ᵏ⁾ + δχ*
    control = control + step.value  # (N,)

# S χ*
final_increment = prior_sqrt.mv(control)  # (N,)
# x₀* = x_b + S χ*
analysis_by_hand = background + final_increment  # (N,)
print(bool(jnp.allclose(analysis_by_hand, analysis[0], atol=1e-4)))

records.content:
Three multiplicative speedups over StrongFourDVar with NonlinearCG:

CVT preconditioning. CG converges in O(10) iterations instead of O(\sqrt{\kappa(B)}), where \kappa(B) is the prior condition number.

Linearisation reuse. The tangent linear M' is computed once per outer iteration and reused across all n_\text{inner} inner CG steps, whereas NonlinearCG on the full nonlinear cost recomputes the gradient (a full forward and adjoint pass) at every step.

Cheap posterior. The posterior precision is the operator the inner loop solves with (see the posterior section below).

For a typical operational problem (T = 12 hours, n = 10^7 grid
points, m = 10^5 observations), IncrementalFourDVar converges in
minutes; StrongFourDVar with NonlinearCG takes hours.

For T = 0 and linear H, IncrementalFourDVar must agree with OptimalInterpolation (the Decision D14 invariant, see 

chapter 4): the outer iteration converges in one step (no relinearisation needed), and the inner CG produces the BLUE 

(4.4). The block continues the one above:

# Shapes: S = 1 window; T = 1 time; N = 4 cells


# user
class Static(eqx.Module):
    """M(x) = x: a single-time window reduces 4DVar to OI."""

    dt: float = 1.0

    def step(self, state: Float[Array, " n"], dt: float) -> Float[Array, " n"]:
        # M(x) = x
        return state


# diag(B) = 2
static_prior_diag = jnp.full(4, 2.0)  # (N,)
# diag(R) = 1/2
static_obs_diag = jnp.full(4, 0.5)  # (N,)
# B = 2 I, over the (N,) state of 4DVar
static_prior_cov = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(static_prior_diag)  # (N, N) op
# R = I / 2
static_obs_cov = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(static_obs_diag)  # (N, N) op
# the same B and R over OI's (T, N) state
field_prior_diag = jnp.full((1, 4), 2.0)  # (T, N)
field_obs_diag = jnp.full((1, 4), 0.5)  # (T, N)
field_prior_cov = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(field_prior_diag)  # (T N, T N) op
field_obs_cov = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(field_obs_diag)  # (T N, T N) op
# y = (1, 2, 3, 4)
single_obs = jnp.arange(1.0, 5.0)  # (N,)
single_window = einx.id("n -> 1 1 n", single_obs)  # (N,) → (S, T, N)
# m = 1 everywhere
single_mask = jnp.ones((1, 1, 4))  # (S, T, N)
# today (vardax)
single_batch = vdx.Batch1D(input=single_window, mask=single_mask)
# today (vardax)
# p(x) = 𝒩(0, B), p(y | x) = 𝒩(x, R)
optimal_interpolation = vdx.OptimalInterpolation(
    obs_op=vdx.MaskedIdentity(),
    prior_mean=jnp.zeros((1, 4)),
    prior_cov_op=field_prior_cov,
    obs_cov_op=field_obs_cov,
)
# today (vardax)
# (I + Sᵀ R⁻¹ S) δχ* = −∇_χ J, with H = M = I
static_incremental = vdx.IncrementalFourDVar(
    forward=Static(),
    obs_op=vdx.MaskedIdentity(),
    prior_mean=jnp.zeros(4),
    prior_cov_op=static_prior_cov,
    obs_cov_op=static_obs_cov,
    config=vdx.IncrementalConfig(n_outer=2, n_inner=50, cvt=True),
)
# today (vardax)
# x_a = x_b + B Hᵀ (H B Hᵀ + R)⁻¹ (y − H x_b)
closed_form = optimal_interpolation(single_batch)  # → (S, T, N)
# today (vardax)
# x₀* after two Gauss-Newton outer loops
gauss_newton = static_incremental(single_batch)  # → (S, N)
print(bool(jnp.allclose(closed_form[:, 0], gauss_newton, atol=1e-3)))

records.content:
Almost never, for operational work. IncrementalFourDVar is faster
and produces the same answer. Use StrongFourDVar only when:

B is large, unstructured and has no cheap square root, so
gaussx.sqrt would fall back to a dense eigendecomposition. Pass a
Lanczos square root (prior_sqrt_op=gaussx.sqrt(B, lanczos_order=k))
or use cvt=False before giving up on the incremental solver.

You want to swap in a custom optimistix minimiser (e.g.
optx.LevenbergMarquardt for very nonlinear cases). Incremental
uses a fixed GN+CG; the rest of the optimistix zoo isn’t compatible
with the incremental machinery.

For most users, IncrementalFourDVar is the right default.

4DVarNet replaces two pieces of classical 4DVar with learned
counterparts: the Gaussian prior \|x - x_b\|^2_{B^{-1}} becomes a
learned reconstruction \|x - \varphi_\theta(x)\|^2, and the inner
gradient-descent solver becomes a learned iteration with a ConvLSTM
gradient modulator. The result is trainable end-to-end on
(input, target) pairs.

The “Net” naming follows Fablet et al. (2021). vardax keeps it as the name of the method, not the family: 4DVarNet is one of seven peer analysis methods (Decision D14), a learned variant of strong-constraint 4DVar distinguished by its learned components, and not the parent of classical 4DVar.

The variational cost is structurally familiar:J(x) = \alpha_\text{obs} \frac{1}{2} \|H(x) - y\|^2_{R^{-1}} + \alpha_\text{prior} \|x - \varphi_\theta(x)\|^2

where the first term is the observation cost 

(2.2), \varphi_\theta is a learned autoencoder with parameters \theta, and \alpha_\text{obs} and \alpha_\text{prior} weight the two terms. The Gaussian background
term \|x - x_b\|^2_{B^{-1}} is replaced (not added). The learned
prior is expressive enough to encode the same information that B +
x_b would, plus structure that classical Gaussian priors can’t
represent (multimodality, nonlinear manifolds, conditional
dependencies).

Classical 4DVar minimises J via gradient descent or a quasi-Newton
method. 4DVarNet replaces the inner step with a learned modulator:x_{k+1} = x_k - \Phi_\phi(\nabla_x J(x_k), h_k), \text{ for } k = 0, \ldots, K-1

where J is the cost 

(9.1), \Phi_\phi is a small neural network (ConvLSTM, MLP, or attention) with parameters \phi, and h_k is its recurrent hidden state. The network sees the current gradient and decides how to step, so it can learn momentum, adaptive step sizes, or problem-specific preconditioning that hand-coded solvers don’t capture.

After K iterations the analysis is x^* = x_K. The whole pipeline (forward, gradient, modulator, update) is differentiable end-to-end.

The training objective minimises reconstruction error against
ground-truth states:\mathcal{L}(\theta, \phi) = \mathbb{E}_{(y, x_\text{true})} \|x^*(\theta, \phi; y) - x_\text{true}\|^2

where x^*(\theta, \phi; y) is the analysis after K steps of 

(9.2) from the observations y, and x_\text{true} is the ground-truth state. The training gradient \nabla_{\theta, \phi} \mathcal{L} flows through
the inner solver. This is where the adjoint choice (Decision D15)
matters.

hierarchy.lvl3: Adjoint choices for the inner solver
Adjoint choices for the inner solver

records.content:
Vardax exposes solver_adjoint: optimistix.AbstractAdjoint as a
constructor slot. Three viable choices:

Adjoint

Memory

Convergence requirement

Notes

optimistix.RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint()

O(K) checkpoints

None

Standard backprop with recursive checkpointing

vardax.adjoints.OneStepAdjoint()

O(1)

None

Bolte et al. 2023; only the last step differentiable

optimistix.ImplicitAdjoint()

O(1)

Yes

IFT-based at the fixed point; exact at convergence

RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint is the default. It backpropagates through all K unrolled steps, with recursive checkpointing to bound memory, so it always works and costs O(K) checkpoints.

OneStepAdjoint runs K-1 steps with jax.lax.stop_gradient applied to the trajectory, then a single differentiable step, so the training gradient picks up only the last iteration’s contribution. Bolte et al. (2023) prove this is exact at convergence; in practice it works well for converged or near-converged inner solvers. Its memory cost is O(1), which makes it the right choice for K \ge 20 when memory is constrained.

vardax ships OneStepAdjoint in vardax._src.adjoints.one_step with
the goal of upstreaming to optimistix once stable (Decision D6).

ImplicitAdjoint uses the implicit function theorem at the fixed point x^* = f(x^*; \theta) of the inner iteration:\frac{d x^*}{d \theta} = \left(I - \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right)^{-1} \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}

where f is the inner-step map 

(9.2) and both partial derivatives are taken at x^*. It is the implicit gradient 

(12.2) of chapter 12 with the stationarity condition replaced by the fixed-point residual x - f(x; \theta) = 0. Memory O(1), gradient exact at
convergence. Requires the inner solver to actually converge; if K is
too small, the IFT gradient is wrong. Use when the inner iteration is
known to be a contraction.

The example below trains a small FourDVarNet2D on S = 4 windows of T = 3 frames on an 8 \times 8 grid, for a few optimiser steps only.
The truth is a travelling wave x_\text{true}(s, t, y, x) = \sin(0.8 y + 0.3 t + \varphi_s) with a random phase \varphi_s per window, about half the cells are observed with mask m, and the observations are m \odot x_\text{true}.
The model’s cost is J(x) = \|m \odot (x - y)\|^2 + \lambda \|x - \varphi_\theta(x)\|^2, which is 

(9.1) with H(x) = m \odot x, R = I and no factor ½, and the solver runs 

(9.2) with the modulator output scaled by a step size \alpha.

import einx
import equinox as eqx
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import optax
import vardax as vdx

# Shapes: S = 4 samples; T = 3 times; Y = 8 rows; X = 8 columns

key_model, key_phase, key_mask = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(0), 3)

rows = jnp.arange(8.0)  # (Y,)
times = jnp.arange(3.0)  # (T,)
# φₛ ~ U(0, 2π), one phase per window
phase = jax.random.uniform(key_phase, (4,), maxval=2 * jnp.pi)  # (S,)
# 0.8 y
row_phase = 0.8 * rows  # (Y,)
# 0.3 t
time_phase = 0.3 * times  # (T,)
# 0.8 y + 0.3 t + φₛ
wave_phase = einx.add("y, t, s -> s t y", row_phase, time_phase, phase)  # (S, T, Y)
# x_true(s, t, y) = sin(0.8 y + 0.3 t + φₛ)
wave = jnp.sin(wave_phase)  # (S, T, Y)
# the wave is constant along x
target = einx.id("s t y -> s t y x", wave, x=8)  # (S, T, Y) → (S, T, Y, X)
# m ~ Bernoulli(0.5)
observed = jax.random.bernoulli(key_mask, 0.5, (4, 3, 8, 8))  # (S, T, Y, X)
mask = observed.astype(jnp.float32)  # (S, T, Y, X)
# y = m ⊙ x_true
obs = mask * target  # (S, T, Y, X)

# today (vardax)
batch = vdx.Batch2D(input=obs, mask=mask, target=target)
# today (vardax)
# x_{k+1} = x_k − α Φ_ϕ(∇J(x_k), h_k), K = 3, with a bilinear autoencoder φ_θ
model = vdx.FourDVarNet2D(
    n_time=3,
    height=8,
    width=8,
    latent_dim=4,
    hidden_dim=4,
    n_solver_steps=3,
    alpha=0.2,
    prior_weight=1.0,
    solver_adjoint=vdx.OneStepAdjoint(),
    key=key_model,
)

# today (optax)
optimizer = optax.adam(1e-3)
# the trainable leaves (θ, ϕ)
params = eqx.filter(model, eqx.is_array)
# today (optax)
opt_state = optimizer.init(params)
losses = []
for _ in range(20):
    # today (vardax)
    # (θ, ϕ) ← adam step on ℒ(θ, ϕ) = mean (x*(θ, ϕ; y) − x_true)²
    model, opt_state, loss = vdx.train_step(model, batch, optimizer, opt_state)
    losses.append(float(loss))
print(f"loss {losses[0]:.3f} -> {losses[-1]:.3f}")

IdentityPrior with a fixed-step modulator and many solver steps is the classical baseline, useful for checking agreement with the linear-Gaussian limit (Decision D14 invariant).
With IdentityPrior the prior cost \|x - \varphi(x)\|^2 is zero, and a modulator that passes the gradient through unchanged turns the solver into fixed-step gradient descent on J(x) = \|m \odot (x - y)\|^2.
No such modulator ships, so the block defines one and hands it to solve_4dvarnet_1d; with step \alpha = 0.05 and K = 200 steps it converges to m \odot y.
OptimalInterpolation with x_b = 0, B = I and R = \sigma^2 I gives the same field in the limit \sigma \to 0; here \sigma = 0.01 on N = 8 cells, about 60% of them observed.
The block continues the one above.

from typing import Any

import lineax as lx
from jaxtyping import Array, Float

# Shapes: S = 1 sample; T = 1 time; N = 8 grid cells

key_truth, key_cells = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(1))
state_structure = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((1, 8), jnp.float32)

# B = I
prior_cov = lx.IdentityLinearOperator(state_structure)  # (T N, T N) op
# R = σ² I, σ = 0.01; tagged PSD so the default CG solve accepts it
obs_cov = lx.TaggedLinearOperator(  # (T N, T N) PSD op
    jnp.float32(1e-4) * prior_cov, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
)
# x_true ~ 𝒩(0, I)
truth = jax.random.normal(key_truth, (1, 1, 8))  # (S, T, N)
# m ~ Bernoulli(0.6)
observed_cells = jax.random.bernoulli(key_cells, 0.6, (1, 1, 8))  # (S, T, N)
cell_mask = observed_cells.astype(jnp.float32)  # (S, T, N)
# y = m ⊙ x_true
line_obs = cell_mask * truth  # (S, T, N)
# today (vardax)
line_batch = vdx.Batch1D(input=line_obs, mask=cell_mask)


# user
class FixedStepGradMod(eqx.Module):
    """Pass the gradient through unchanged, so the solver takes fixed steps."""

    def __call__(
        self, grad: Float[Array, "s t n"], state: Float[Array, "s t n"], carry: Any
    ) -> tuple[Float[Array, "s t n"], Any]:
        # Φ(∇J, h) = ∇J
        return grad, carry


# today (vardax)
# φ(x) = x, so ‖x − φ(x)‖² = 0
identity_prior = vdx.IdentityPrior()
# user
grad_mod = FixedStepGradMod()
# today (vardax)
# x_{k+1} = x_k − α ∇J(x_k), with J(x) = ‖m ⊙ (x − y)‖²
descent = vdx.solve_4dvarnet_1d(  # → (S, T, N)
    line_batch,
    identity_prior,
    grad_mod,
    n_steps=200,
    hidden_dim=1,
    alpha=0.05,
)
# today (vardax)
# p(x) = 𝒩(0, B), p(y | x) = 𝒩(m ⊙ x, R)
optimal_interpolation = vdx.OptimalInterpolation(
    obs_op=vdx.MaskedIdentity(),
    prior_mean=jnp.zeros((1, 8)),
    prior_cov_op=prior_cov,
    obs_cov_op=obs_cov,
)
# today (vardax)
# x_a = x_b + B Hᵀ (H B Hᵀ + R)⁻¹ (y − H x_b)
closed_form = optimal_interpolation(line_batch)  # → (S, T, N)
print(bool(jnp.allclose(descent, closed_form, atol=1e-2)))

Program 9.2:Runs 

(9.2) with Φ(∇J, h) = ∇J and an identity prior, and checks it against the BLUE mean 

(4.4).

It prints True.

This is the floor. A trained FourDVarNet with a non-trivial prior and grad modulator typically does better in nonlinear regimes, but the floor confirms the implementation is correct.

Use FourDVarNet when:

You have a training set of (observation, ground-truth) pairs

The classical B is hard to specify or known to be inadequate

The regime is data-rich and learning-friendly (smooth manifolds, no
catastrophic distribution shift between train and test)

Don’t use FourDVarNet when:

You have no training pairs; go with classical methods (chapters 4 to 8)

The training distribution doesn’t match deployment, since FourDVarNet extrapolates poorly outside its training manifold

You need defensible posterior covariance, since the Laplace approximation 

(13.1) around a learned-prior MAP can be miscalibrated; IncrementalFourDVar with a classical Matérn prior gives a more honest posterior

LaplaceCovariance builds its Hessian from the model’s obs_op, B and R, which FourDVarNet2D does not have, so it raises AttributeError on this model.
The Laplace approximation of the learned cost is assembled by hand instead: with residuals r(x) = (m \odot (x - y), \sqrt{\lambda} (x - \varphi_\theta(x))) and Jacobian J_r at the analysis x^*, the Gauss-Newton Hessian is \nabla^2 J \approx 2 J_r^\top J_r and the Laplace covariance 

(13.1) is P^* = (\nabla^2 J)^{-1}, applied by a CG solve.
The block continues the first one on this page, for its first window, with \lambda = 1.

# Shapes: S = 1 sample; T = 3 times; Y = 8 rows; X = 8 columns

first_obs = obs[:1]  # (S, T, Y, X)
first_mask = mask[:1]  # (S, T, Y, X)
# today (vardax)
one_window = vdx.Batch2D(input=first_obs, mask=first_mask)
# today (vardax)
# x* = x_K
analysis = model(one_window)  # → (S, T, Y, X)


# user
def residuals(
    state: Float[Array, "s t y x"],
) -> tuple[Float[Array, "s t y x"], Float[Array, "s t y x"]]:
    """The residuals r(x) = (m ⊙ (x − y), √λ (x − φ_θ(x))), λ = 1."""
    # x − y
    misfit = state - one_window.input  # (S, T, Y, X)
    # r_o = m ⊙ (x − y)
    obs_residual = one_window.mask * misfit  # (S, T, Y, X)
    # today (vardax)
    # φ_θ(x)
    reconstruction = model.prior(state)  # (S, T, Y, X)
    # r_p = √λ (x − φ_θ(x)), λ = 1
    prior_residual = state - reconstruction  # (S, T, Y, X)
    return obs_residual, prior_residual


# δx ↦ J_r δx at x*
_, residual_jvp = jax.linearize(residuals, analysis)
# δr ↦ J_rᵀ δr
residual_vjp = jax.linear_transpose(residual_jvp, analysis)


# user
def precision_mv(direction: Float[Array, "s t y x"]) -> Float[Array, "s t y x"]:
    """The Gauss-Newton Hessian product ∇²J δx ≈ 2 J_rᵀ J_r δx."""
    # J_r δx
    residual_direction = residual_jvp(direction)
    # J_rᵀ J_r δx
    (pulled_back,) = residual_vjp(residual_direction)  # (S, T, Y, X)
    # ∇²J δx ≈ 2 J_rᵀ J_r δx
    return 2.0 * pulled_back  # (S, T, Y, X)


analysis_structure = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct(analysis.shape, analysis.dtype)
# ∇²J ≈ 2 J_rᵀ J_r
posterior_precision = lx.FunctionLinearOperator(  # (S T Y X, S T Y X) PSD op
    precision_mv, analysis_structure, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
)
# 1
ones = jnp.ones_like(analysis)  # (S, T, Y, X)
precision_solver = lx.CG(rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-5, max_steps=500)
# today (lineax)
# P* 1 = (∇²J)⁻¹ 1, one matrix-free solve
spread = lx.linear_solve(  # (S, T, Y, X) → (S, T, Y, X)
    posterior_precision, ones, solver=precision_solver
)
print(spread.value.shape, int(spread.stats["num_steps"]))

4DVarNet originated as a research line (Fablet et al. 2021, 2023) that
demonstrated end-to-end learning of variational DA on satellite SSH.
The original codebase (CIA-Oceanix/4dvarnet-starter) is PyTorch and
ocean-specific. Vardax brings the same algorithm into JAX, peers it
with the classical DA hierarchy, and connects it to the broader
ecosystem (somax / plumax for physics, gaussx for structured priors,
filterax for hybrid EnVar, pipekit-cycle for orchestration).

In the v0.4 design the classical methods are the foundation, not legacy, and 4DVarNet earns its place beside them as a useful learned variant.

The six methods covered so far (chapters 4 to 9) all solve a fresh minimisation per event. A new observation triggers a new analysis, which is fine for retrospective work but too slow for real-time. Amortized
inference learns a function q_\phi(x \mid y) that maps observations
directly to posteriors, in a single forward pass.

The cost of training amortizes over many events; the per-event cost
becomes a single neural network evaluation. This is the difference
between research and operations.

Learn a conditional density q_\phi(x \mid y) that approximates the exact Bayesian posterior 

(1.1):\phi^* = \underset{\phi}{\arg\min} \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p(y)} \mathrm{KL}\left(q_\phi(\cdot \mid y) \| p(\cdot \mid y)\right)

where \phi are the network parameters and the expectation runs over the observations the model will see.

When the prior and forward model are samplable (which they are when
supplied by somax or plumax), the training distribution comes from
simulation:

Draw x \sim p(x) from the prior.

Simulate y = H(M(x)) + \varepsilon, the observation model 

(2.1) applied to the forecast M(x).

Train q_\phi to recover x from y on these synthetic pairs.

This is “simulation-based inference” (Cranmer et al. 2020). The training distribution is fully controlled (every (x, y) pair has known ground truth), but the deployment distribution must match for q_\phi to be calibrated.

vardax AmortizedPosterior exposes three head choices via the
head_type config:

Learn an invertible map f_\phi from a base Gaussian to the
posterior, conditioned on the observation context:x = f_\phi(z; c_\psi(y)), \text{ with } z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)

where c_\psi(y) is the context vector from an observation encoder with parameters \psi. The change of variables gives the density\log q_\phi(x \mid y) = \log p_z\left(f_\phi^{-1}(x; c_\psi(y))\right) - \log \left| \det \partial f_\phi / \partial z \right|

where p_z is the base Gaussian density and the Jacobian is taken at z = f_\phi^{-1}(x; c_\psi(y)).

Exact density, exact samples. Use gauss_flows for the flow
implementation. Good for moderate-dimensional state (up to \sim 10^4).
Higher-dimensional flows are open research.

Learn the score of a noise-perturbed posterior at noise scale t:s_\phi(x, t \mid y) \approx \nabla_x \log p_t(x \mid y)

where p_t is the posterior perturbed by noise up to scale t. Sampling runs the reverse SDEd x = \left[f(x, t) - g(t)^2 s_\phi(x, t \mid y) \right] d t + g(t) d \bar{w}

backwards in t, where f and g are the drift and diffusion of the forward noising process and \bar{w} is a reverse-time Wiener process.

No exact density (sampling-only). High capacity for multimodal posteriors, since the diffusion process can represent disconnected components, which flows struggle with. Scales to higher state dimensions than flows.

Predict Gaussian posterior parameters directly:q_\phi(x \mid y) = \mathcal{N}\left(x; \mu_\phi(y), \Sigma_\phi(y)\right)

where \mu_\phi and \Sigma_\phi are the network’s predicted posterior mean and covariance.

Cheapest by far. Restricted to unimodal Gaussian posteriors. Useful when the posterior is known to be Gaussian (e.g., as a learned replacement for the Laplace approximation 

(13.1) around an IncrementalFourDVar MAP).

Flow and regression heads use maximum likelihood on simulated pairs:\mathcal{L}_\text{MLE}(\phi) = -\mathbb{E}_{(x, y) \sim p_\text{sim}} \log q_\phi(x \mid y)

where p_\text{sim} is the joint distribution of the simulated pairs. Score heads use denoising score matching:\mathcal{L}_\text{DSM}(\phi) = \mathbb{E}_{t, x, y, \varepsilon} \left\| s_\phi(x_t, t \mid y) - \nabla_{x_t} \log p_t(x_t \mid x) \right\|^2

where x_t = x + \sigma(t)\varepsilon is the noised state, \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), and \sigma(t) is the noise scale at t.

Both reduce to a standard training step over simulated minibatches: amortized_train_step is chapter 9’s train_step with the negative log-likelihood 

(10.7) in place of the reconstruction loss 

(9.3).

Only the regression head ships today: ConditionalFlowHead and ScoreDiffusionHead are stubs that raise NotImplementedError when constructed, so the example uses RegressionHead.
The toy problem has a state of T = 1 time and N = 4 cells with prior p(x) = \mathcal{N}(0, I) and observations y = x + \sigma \varepsilon, \sigma = 0.5, fully observed.
Its exact posterior is \mathcal{N}(y / (1 + \sigma^2), \sigma^2 / (1 + \sigma^2) I), the BLUE 

(4.4) and 

(4.5) with B = I, H = I and R = \sigma^2 I, which the trained head should recover.
Each training step draws S = 64 fresh simulated pairs, and the head is the Gaussian head 

(10.6) with diagonal covariance.

import einx
import equinox as eqx
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import optax
import vardax as vdx
from jaxtyping import Array, Float, PRNGKeyArray

# Shapes: S = 64 simulated pairs; T = 1 time; N = 4 grid cells; C = 16 context

key_encoder, key_head, key_train, key_test, key_samples = jax.random.split(
    jax.random.PRNGKey(0), 5
)
obs_std = 0.5  # σ


# user
def sample_train_pair(
    key: PRNGKeyArray,
) -> tuple[Float[Array, "t n"], Float[Array, "t n"]]:
    """Draw one simulated pair (x, y) from the prior and the observation model."""
    key_state, key_noise = jax.random.split(key)
    # x ~ p(x) = 𝒩(0, I)
    state = jax.random.normal(key_state, (1, 4))  # (T, N)
    # ε ~ 𝒩(0, I)
    noise = jax.random.normal(key_noise, (1, 4))  # (T, N)
    # y = x + σ ε
    obs = state + obs_std * noise  # (T, N)
    return state, obs


# user
@eqx.filter_jit
def simulate_batch(key: PRNGKeyArray) -> vdx.Batch1D:
    """Draw S simulated pairs as a fully observed batch."""
    pair_keys = jax.random.split(key, 64)
    states, obs = jax.vmap(sample_train_pair)(pair_keys)  # (S, T, N)
    # m = 1 everywhere
    all_observed = jnp.ones_like(obs)  # (S, T, N)
    # today (vardax)
    return vdx.Batch1D(input=obs, mask=all_observed, target=states)


# today (vardax)
# c = MLP([vec(y); vec(m)])
encoder = vdx.MLPObsEncoder(input_size=4, context_dim=16, key=key_encoder)
# today (vardax)
# q_φ(x | y) = 𝒩(μ_φ(c), diag σ²_φ(c))
head = vdx.RegressionHead(context_dim=16, state_shape=(1, 4), key=key_head)
# today (vardax)
config = vdx.AmortizedConfig(head_type="regression", n_samples=64)
# today (vardax)
# x ↦ q_φ(x | y), one encoder pass and one head pass
model = vdx.AmortizedPosterior(encoder=encoder, head=head, config=config)

# today (optax)
optimizer = optax.adam(3e-3)
# the trainable leaves φ
params = eqx.filter(model, eqx.is_array)
# today (optax)
opt_state = optimizer.init(params)
for batch_key in jax.random.split(key_train, 1000):
    batch = simulate_batch(batch_key)
    # today (vardax)
    # ℒ_MLE(φ) = −mean log q_φ(x | y)
    model, opt_state, loss = vdx.amortized_train_step(
        model, batch, optimizer, opt_state
    )
print(f"final NLL {float(loss):.2f}")

# inference: one forward pass per batch
test_batch = simulate_batch(key_test)
# today (vardax)
# x* = μ_φ(y), the mode of q_φ(x | y)
x_map = model(test_batch)  # → (S, T, N)
# today (vardax)
# xⱼ ~ q_φ(x | y), j = 1, …, 200
samples = model.sample(test_batch, key_samples, n=200)  # → (S, 200, T, N)
# today (vardax)
# log q_φ(x | y), exact for the regression head
log_density = model.log_prob(test_batch.target, test_batch)  # → (S,)
# E[x | y] = y / (1 + σ²)
exact_mean = test_batch.input / (1 + obs_std**2)  # (S, T, N)
# x* − E[x | y]
mean_gap = x_map - exact_mean  # (S, T, N)
# |x* − E[x | y]|
abs_mean_gap = jnp.abs(mean_gap)  # (S, T, N)
# max |x* − E[x | y]|
mean_error = einx.max("s t n ->", abs_mean_gap)  # → ()
print(samples.shape, log_density.shape, f"max mean error {float(mean_error):.2f}")

(10.6) by minimising

Amortized inference is dangerous when miscalibrated. A well-trained
flow with a tight q_\phi that’s centred wrong gives confident wrong
answers. Decision D12 (the six-step cycle, chapter 14) requires three
gates before promoting an amortized head to operational use:

The amortized MAP must fall within 1\sigma_\text{post} of an
oracle MAP from a slower method (StrongFourDVar /
IncrementalFourDVar):\frac{|x^*_\text{amort} - x^*_\text{oracle}|}{\sigma_\text{post, oracle}} \le 1

where \sigma_\text{post, oracle} is the oracle’s posterior standard deviation, cell by cell. This is the posterior gate 

(14.4) of chapter 14 applied to the amortized map.

For the toy problem the oracle is ThreeDVar with B = I and R = \sigma^2 I, whose Laplace posterior 

(13.1) is exact here because the problem is linear-Gaussian.
assert_posterior_agreement reads only the mean of the fast posterior, so the amortized MAP goes in a Posterior without a covariance.
The block continues the one above.

import lineax as lx

# Shapes: S = 1 window; T = 1 time; N = 4 grid cells

key_val, key_sbc = jax.random.split(jax.random.PRNGKey(1))
state_structure = jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((1, 4), jnp.float32)
# B = I
prior_cov = lx.IdentityLinearOperator(state_structure)  # (T N, T N) op
# R = σ² I; tagged PSD so the default CG solve accepts it
obs_cov = lx.TaggedLinearOperator(  # (T N, T N) PSD op
    jnp.float32(obs_std**2) * prior_cov, lx.positive_semidefinite_tag
)
# today (vardax)
# J(x) = ½ ‖x‖²_{B⁻¹} + ½ ‖y − x‖²_{R⁻¹}
oracle = vdx.ThreeDVar(
    obs_op=vdx.MaskedIdentity(),
    prior_mean=jnp.zeros((1, 4)),
    prior_cov_op=prior_cov,
    obs_cov_op=obs_cov,
)

val_batch = simulate_batch(key_val)
for window_index in range(4):
    window_obs = val_batch.input[window_index : window_index + 1]  # (S, T, N)
    window_mask = val_batch.mask[window_index : window_index + 1]  # (S, T, N)
    # today (vardax)
    window = vdx.Batch1D(input=window_obs, mask=window_mask)
    # today (vardax)
    # P* = (B⁻¹ + Hᵀ R⁻¹ H)⁻¹ at the 3DVar MAP
    p_oracle = oracle.posterior(window)
    # today (vardax)
    # x*_amort = μ_φ(y)
    amortized_map = model(window)  # → (S, T, N)
    # today (vardax)
    p_amort = vdx.Posterior(mean=amortized_map[0])
    # today (vardax)
    # |x*_amort − x*_oracle| / σ_oracle ≤ 1, cell by cell
    vdx.assert_posterior_agreement(p_amort, p_oracle, tolerance_sigma=1.0)
print("posterior agreement passed")

Program 10.2:Checks the posterior-agreement gate 

(10.9) for the amortized MAP against a 3DVar oracle with the Laplace posterior 

(13.1), on four windows.

It prints posterior agreement passed.

The amortized model’s gradient with respect to observations must match
the physics-based gradient:\frac{\|\partial x^*_\text{amort} / \partial y - \partial x^*_\text{oracle} / \partial y\|_\text{op}}{\|\partial x^*_\text{oracle} / \partial y\|_\text{op}} < 0.05

where \|\cdot\|_\text{op} is the operator norm. This is the Jacobian gate 

(14.3) of chapter 14 applied to the amortized map, with y as the input. It is measured by random-vector probing (randomised tangent-linear tests for operator agreement). Without this gate, the amortized model may match the oracle MAP on the training distribution but extrapolate badly when the observation distribution shifts.

Per Talts et al. (2018): sample x^{(j)} from the prior, simulate
y^{(j)}, draw q_\phi samples conditioned on y^{(j)}, compute the
rank of x^{(j)} in the sample. If q_\phi is calibrated, the ranks
are uniform across the sample. Failure indicates over- or
under-confident posteriors.

simulation_based_calibration takes three callables (posterior sampler, prior sampler, simulator) rather than the model, and reduces each state to its \ell_2 norm before ranking it among the samples.
With 19 samples per run the rank takes 20 values, grouped here into 5 bins of 4; a calibrated head gives about 20 runs per bin.
The block continues the one above.

import jax.scipy.stats as jstats

# Shapes: T = 1 time; N = 4 grid cells; J = 19 posterior samples per run


# user
@eqx.filter_jit
def sample_posterior(
    obs: Float[Array, "t n"], key: PRNGKeyArray, n: int
) -> Float[Array, "j t n"]:
    """Draw n samples from q_φ(x | y) for one fully observed window."""
    obs_window = einx.id("t n -> 1 t n", obs)  # (T, N) → (1, T, N)
    # m = 1 everywhere
    all_observed = jnp.ones_like(obs_window)  # (1, T, N)
    # today (vardax)
    window = vdx.Batch1D(input=obs_window, mask=all_observed)
    # today (vardax)
    # xⱼ ~ q_φ(x | y)
    window_samples = model.sample(window, key, n)  # → (1, J, T, N)
    return window_samples[0]  # (1, J, T, N) → (J, T, N)


# user
def sample_prior(key: PRNGKeyArray) -> Float[Array, "t n"]:
    """Draw x from the prior p(x)."""
    # x ~ 𝒩(0, I)
    return jax.random.normal(key, (1, 4))  # (T, N)


# user
def simulate_obs(state: Float[Array, "t n"], key: PRNGKeyArray) -> Float[Array, "t n"]:
    """Simulate y from x through the observation model."""
    # ε ~ 𝒩(0, I)
    noise = jax.random.normal(key, (1, 4))  # (T, N)
    # y = x + σ ε
    return state + obs_std * noise  # (T, N)


# today (vardax)
# rank of ‖x‖ among ‖xⱼ‖, xⱼ ~ q_φ(x | y), over 100 runs
ranks = vdx.simulation_based_calibration(  # → (100,)
    sample_posterior,
    sample_prior,
    simulate_obs,
    key=key_sbc,
    n_runs=100,
    n_samples=19,
)
# b = ⌊rank / 4⌋, five bins of four ranks
rank_bins = ranks // 4  # (100,)
# n_b, the runs in bin b
bin_counts = jnp.bincount(rank_bins, length=5)  # (100,) → (5,)
# (n_b − 20)²
squared_excess = (bin_counts - 20) ** 2  # (5,)
# χ² = Σ_b (n_b − 20)² / 20
chi_square = einx.sum("b ->", squared_excess) / 20  # → ()
# p = P(χ²₄ ≥ χ²)
p_value = jstats.chi2.sf(chi_square, 4)  # → ()
print(bin_counts.tolist(), f"chi2 p = {float(p_value):.3f}")

The right pattern is both: use solver-based methods to produce
oracle posteriors on a representative sample, train an amortized head
against the oracle, validate via the gates, then deploy the head for
real-time work. The six-step cycle (chapter 14) formalises this.

Chapter 2 introduced the observation model 

(2.1), its cost 

(2.2) and the ObservationOperator protocol, and it defines each operator family. This chapter is the catalogue of the operators vardax ships (masked identity, linear projection, averaging kernel, multi-instrument fusion and scattered point observations) and of their implementation details.

The first four satisfy pipekit_cycle.ObservationOperator (the first three directly; multi-instrument fusion via its .to_observation_operator() adapter, see chapter 2), which tests/test_pipekit_protocols.py checks. These four expose __call__(x) and linearize(x); the adjoint test at the end of this chapter checks the tangent-linear contract.

The Python blocks on this page run in order, each continuing the ones above it.

The masked identity 

(2.3) observes the state where m_i = 1. The PRNG keys for the whole page are split here.

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import vardax as vdx

# Shapes: N = 6 grid cells

key = jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
(
    key_state,
    key_mask,
    key_left,
    key_right,
    key_tropomi,
    key_emit,
    key_truth,
    key_noise,
    key_adjoint,
) = jax.random.split(key, 9)

# x ~ 𝒩(0, I)
state = jax.random.normal(key_state, (6,))  # (N,)
# m ~ Bernoulli(0.5)
is_observed = jax.random.bernoulli(key_mask, 0.5, (6,))  # (N,) bool
mask = is_observed.astype(jnp.float32)  # (N,)

# today (vardax)
masked_op = vdx.MaskedIdentity()
# today (vardax)
# H(x) = m ⊙ x
predicted = masked_op(state, mask=mask)  # (N,) → (N,)
# today (vardax)
# H′(x) = I; the mask enters at call time, not in the tangent
tangent = masked_op.linearize(state)  # (N, N) op
# H′ m = m
tangent_mask = tangent.mv(mask)  # (N,) → (N,)
print(type(tangent).__name__, bool(jnp.allclose(tangent_mask, mask)))

Program 11.1:Applies the masked identity 

(2.3) to a random state and reads its tangent H′(x).

It prints JacobianLinearOperator True: the tangent is the identity, so masked residuals come from the cost, which multiplies by m.

The mask can be soft (m_i \in [0, 1]) for fuzzy observations. The operator still works, but the obs-error covariance interpretation changes (a soft mask implicitly inflates R where m is small).

The linear projection 

(2.4) applies a stored matrix H_\text{mat}. The block builds it from a footprint in which each of M = 3 receptors averages two neighbouring cells.

import lineax as lx

# Shapes: M = 3 receptors; N = 6 grid cells

# [½ ½], one receptor over two neighbouring cells
pair_average = jnp.array([[0.5, 0.5]])  # (1, 2)
# H_mat = I₃ ⊗ [½ ½]
footprint = jnp.kron(jnp.eye(3), pair_average)  # (M, N)
footprint_op = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(footprint)  # (M, N) op

# today (vardax)
linear_op = vdx.LinearObs(operator=footprint_op)
# today (vardax)
# H(x) = H_mat x
predicted = linear_op(state)  # (N,) → (M,)
# today (vardax)
# H′(x) = H_mat, the stored operator itself
tangent = linear_op.linearize(state)  # (M, N) op
print(predicted.shape, tangent is linear_op.operator)

Program 11.2:Builds a footprint matrix H_mat and applies the linear projection 

(2.4) and its tangent.

It prints (3,) True.

Use cases:

Lagrangian footprint: a particle simulator produces a footprint matrix mapping the source field to receptor observations. The matrix is often sparse (only cells with non-zero footprint contribute), and lineax has no sparse operator, so wrap the sparse product in a lineax.FunctionLinearOperator.

Spectral filtering: observe specific frequency bands. Store H_\text{mat} = F^{-1} S F as a composition of lineax operators.

Spatial interpolation: bilinear or bicubic projection from the grid to observation points. The interpolation matrix is sparse.

The averaging kernel 

(2.5) is the right model for RTM-derived L2 satellite products; chapter 2 defines it and its symbols, and this section covers its construction and structure. For column CH₄ the weighting h tends to 1 in the lower troposphere, where the signal comes from the atmosphere, and to 0 in the stratosphere, where the retrieval prior x_a takes over. The tangent-linear map H'(x) = A \cdot \mathrm{diag}(h) inherits the structure of A (sparse, Kronecker, low-rank).

L2 products typically include the averaging-kernel matrix, prior, and weighting as sidecar metadata in the netCDF / HDF5 file.

import xarray as xr

# Shapes: L = 4 retrieval levels


# user
def averaging_kernel_from_l2(dataset: xr.Dataset) -> vdx.AveragingKernel:
    # A, dense from the sidecar matrix
    kernel_values = jnp.asarray(dataset["averaging_kernel"].values)  # (L, L)
    kernel = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(kernel_values)  # (L, L) op
    # x_a, the retrieval prior
    prior_profile = jnp.asarray(dataset["retrieval_prior"].values)  # (L,)
    # h, the pressure weighting
    pressure_weights = jnp.asarray(dataset["weighting_vector"].values)  # (L,)
    # today (vardax)
    # H(x) = A (h ⊙ x + (1 − h) ⊙ x_a)
    return vdx.AveragingKernel(
        kernel_matrix=kernel,
        prior_profile=prior_profile,
        pressure_weights=pressure_weights,
    )


# a toy L2 sidecar: smoothing kernel, flat prior, weights falling with height
level_matrix = jnp.array(
    [
        [0.6, 0.3, 0.1, 0.0],
        [0.2, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1],
        [0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 0.2],
        [0.0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.6],
    ]
)  # (L, L)
l2_sidecar = xr.Dataset(
    {
        "averaging_kernel": (("level", "level_out"), level_matrix),
        "retrieval_prior": ("level", jnp.full(4, 1.9)),
        "weighting_vector": ("level", jnp.array([1.0, 0.9, 0.6, 0.2])),
    }
)
# user
tropomi = averaging_kernel_from_l2(l2_sidecar)
# x = 2 on every level
column = jnp.full(4, 2.0)  # (L,)
# ŷ = A (h ⊙ x + (1 − h) ⊙ x_a)
predicted_column = tropomi(column)  # (L,) → (L,)
print(predicted_column)

Program 11.3:Builds the averaging kernel 

(2.5) from a toy L2 sidecar and applies it to a flat column.

It prints [1.993     1.979     1.962     1.9390001]: each row of A sums to one, so the output lies between the state x = 2 and the retrieval prior x_a = 1.9, closer to the prior where h is small.

For separable kernels (e.g. independent vertical and horizontal smoothing), use Kronecker structure, A = A_v \otimes A_h, here with h = 0.8 and x_a = 0.

import einx
import gaussx as gx

# Shapes: L = 2 levels; C = 3 columns; N = L C = 6 cells

# A_v, vertical smoothing
vertical_kernel = jnp.array([[0.7, 0.3], [0.3, 0.7]])  # (L, L)
# A_h, horizontal smoothing
horizontal_kernel = jnp.array(
    [[0.8, 0.2, 0.0], [0.1, 0.8, 0.1], [0.0, 0.2, 0.8]]
)  # (C, C)
vertical_op = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(vertical_kernel)  # (L, L) op
horizontal_op = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(horizontal_kernel)  # (C, C) op
# today (gaussx)
# A = A_v ⊗ A_h
kronecker_kernel = gx.Kronecker(vertical_op, horizontal_op)  # (N, N) op
# today (vardax)
# H(x) = A (h ⊙ x + (1 − h) ⊙ x_a)
separable_ak = vdx.AveragingKernel(
    kernel_matrix=kronecker_kernel,
    prior_profile=jnp.zeros(6),
    pressure_weights=jnp.full(6, 0.8),
)
# today (vardax)
# vec(A_v X A_hᵀ) without forming the (N, N) matrix
smoothed = separable_ak(state)  # (N,) → (N,)
# A = A_v ⊗ A_h, dense for the check
dense_kernel = jnp.kron(vertical_kernel, horizontal_kernel)  # (N, N)
# h ⊙ x with h = 0.8 and x_a = 0
weighted_state = 0.8 * state  # (N,)
# A (h ⊙ x)
dense_smoothed = einx.dot("i j, j -> i", dense_kernel, weighted_state)  # (N,)
print(bool(jnp.allclose(smoothed, dense_smoothed, atol=1e-6)))

Program 11.4:Applies the averaging kernel 

(2.5) with a Kronecker kernel A = A_v ⊗ A_h and checks it against the dense product.

It prints True.

With Kronecker structure A is never materialised, and the mat-vec \mathrm{vec}(A \cdot X) becomes two small mat-vecs instead of one giant one.

For low-rank kernels (information content \le rank), use low-rank
operators:

# Shapes: N = 6 cells; K = 2 rank

# U ~ 𝒩(0, I)
left_vectors = jax.random.normal(key_left, (6, 2))  # (N, K)
# s
singular_values = jnp.array([0.9, 0.4])  # (K,)
# V ~ 𝒩(0, I)
right_vectors = jax.random.normal(key_right, (6, 2))  # (N, K)
# Vᵀ
right_transposed = einx.id("n k -> k n", right_vectors)  # (N, K) → (K, N)
left_op = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(left_vectors)  # (N, K) op
singular_op = lx.DiagonalLinearOperator(singular_values)  # (K, K) op
right_op = lx.MatrixLinearOperator(right_transposed)  # (K, N) op
# A = U diag(s) Vᵀ, composed lazily
low_rank_kernel = left_op @ singular_op @ right_op  # (N, N) op
# A x
low_rank_smoothed = low_rank_kernel.mv(state)  # (N,) → (N,)
print(low_rank_smoothed.shape)

Program 11.5:Composes a lazy low-rank kernel A = U diag(s) Vᵀ for the averaging kernel 

(2.5).

It prints (6,).

Both save memory and respect the underlying retrieval physics (retrievals with low DOF should have low-rank A).
